# Project Proposal: Enterprise Deployment of an Internal AI Assistant

## Background

The organization’s 5,000 employees rely on a wide range of information sources, business applications, policies, procedures, and subject-matter experts to complete daily work. As the organization grows, employees spend increasing amounts of time searching for information, interpreting internal guidance, drafting routine communications, summarizing documents, and navigating operational processes. This creates avoidable delays, inconsistent outputs, and duplicated effort across departments.

Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence make it possible to provide employees with a secure, centrally managed assistant that can help locate and synthesize internal information, draft and revise content, summarize meetings and documents, support analysis, and guide users through approved business processes. A carefully governed internal AI assistant can improve productivity while preserving organizational standards for privacy, security, compliance, and human oversight.

This proposal recommends a phased deployment of an internal AI assistant to the organization’s 5,000 employees. The program will begin with well-defined, lower-risk use cases and expand as the organization develops confidence in the technology, governance model, data quality, and user practices.

## Objectives

The primary objective is to provide employees with a trusted, secure, and accessible AI assistant that reduces time spent on routine knowledge work and improves access to organizational information.

The program will pursue the following objectives:

- Improve employee productivity by supporting research, drafting, summarization, analysis, and routine administrative work.
- Make approved internal knowledge easier to discover and use across departments.
- Reduce duplicated effort and improve consistency in documents, communications, and recurring workflows.
- Establish enterprise standards for responsible AI use, including privacy, security, records management, accessibility, and human review.
- Create a scalable technical and operating foundation for future AI-enabled applications.
- Measure business value through adoption, time savings, user satisfaction, quality, risk indicators, and operational outcomes.
- Build employee capability through training, clear guidance, and ongoing support.

The assistant will augment employees rather than replace accountability or professional judgment. Users will remain responsible for reviewing AI-generated content, validating important information, and making decisions within their delegated authority.

## Scope

The initial deployment will provide a centrally managed AI assistant accessible through the organization’s approved collaboration and productivity environment. Depending on the selected platform, the assistant may support conversational questions, document summarization, drafting, rewriting, translation, brainstorming, structured analysis, meeting follow-up, and retrieval of approved internal information.

The first release will prioritize lower-risk use cases with broad applicability, including:

- Finding and summarizing policies, procedures, standards, and internal guidance.
- Drafting and editing emails, reports, presentations, announcements, and other business communications.
- Summarizing meetings, documents, and lengthy correspondence.
- Creating first drafts of project plans, briefing materials, frequently asked questions, and status updates.
- Supporting research and comparison of internally approved information.
- Helping employees navigate common processes and identify relevant forms, systems, or contacts.
- Assisting with basic data interpretation where the underlying data is authorized, reliable, and appropriately protected.

The program will include role-based access controls, integration with approved identity and collaboration systems, usage monitoring, administrative controls, user training, support procedures, and a governance framework.

The initial scope will not include autonomous decision-making, unsupervised external communications, automated approval of transactions, unrestricted access to confidential or regulated data, or use cases that could materially affect employment, legal rights, safety, financial eligibility, or customer outcomes without appropriate human review and separately approved controls. High-risk integrations and automated actions may be evaluated during later phases, subject to formal risk assessment and executive approval.

The program will also establish standards for data classification, prompt and output handling, retention, auditability, incident reporting, model evaluation, vendor management, and acceptable use. Existing information governance and cybersecurity policies will remain in effect and will be updated where necessary to address AI-specific risks.

## Delivery Approach and Timeline

The deployment will be delivered over approximately twelve months, followed by continuous improvement and expansion.

During months one and two, the project team will establish the program foundation. This phase will confirm executive sponsorship, define governance, select or validate the technology platform, document business and technical requirements, assess privacy and security implications, identify priority use cases, and establish baseline measures for productivity, search effort, user satisfaction, and support demand. The team will also complete an inventory of relevant internal knowledge sources and identify content that requires remediation before it can be connected to the assistant.

During months three and four, the organization will configure and test the initial service. Work will include identity integration, access controls, data-source configuration, logging, content filtering, user-interface design, support processes, and administrator training. Representative users from business, technology, legal, security, human resources, finance, operations, and communications will participate in structured testing. The project team will evaluate response quality, source attribution, access boundaries, harmful or misleading outputs, accessibility, latency, and system reliability.

During months five and six, the organization will conduct a controlled pilot involving approximately 250 to 400 employees across selected departments. Pilot users will receive mandatory training and clear guidance on approved and prohibited uses. The project team will collect quantitative and qualitative feedback, monitor usage and support requirements, test incident-response procedures, and refine the assistant’s configuration and knowledge sources. Pilot results will be reviewed against predefined readiness criteria before broader deployment.

During months seven through nine, the assistant will be expanded to approximately 1,500 employees in waves. Each wave will include communications, role-specific training, manager enablement, office hours, and support coverage. The rollout will prioritize teams with clear use cases, strong data readiness, and leaders prepared to reinforce responsible adoption. Usage, quality, security, and employee feedback will be reviewed after each wave.

During months ten through twelve, the assistant will be made available to the remaining employees, subject to the results of the preceding phases. The program team will finalize enterprise operating procedures, transition routine administration to permanent owners, publish performance dashboards, and recommend the next set of integrations and higher-value use cases. A formal post-implementation review will assess outcomes, risks, costs, and opportunities for expansion.

After the first year, the assistant will operate as an established enterprise service with quarterly governance reviews, ongoing model and configuration evaluations, recurring user training, periodic access reviews, and a prioritized roadmap for new capabilities.

## Resource Requirements

The program will require executive sponsorship from a senior leader with authority across business, technology, risk, and people functions. A steering committee should include representatives from information technology, cybersecurity, privacy, legal, records and information management, human resources, communications, accessibility, finance, operations, and major business units. The steering committee will approve scope, risk tolerance, funding, launch decisions, and future expansion.

A dedicated core team of approximately 12 to 18 full-time equivalent staff will be required during implementation, supplemented by part-time subject-matter experts. Core roles should include a program director, product manager, enterprise architect, AI or machine-learning specialist, security architect, privacy and compliance lead, data and knowledge-management specialists, integration engineers, user-experience and accessibility specialists, change-management and communications leads, training developers, service-desk representatives, and measurement and analytics support.

Business-unit representatives will contribute to use-case prioritization, content validation, pilot testing, and adoption activities. A network of departmental AI champions should be established to provide peer support, identify emerging needs, reinforce acceptable-use practices, and surface risks or improvement opportunities.

The technology budget will cover platform licensing or consumption costs, identity and access integration, secure hosting or vendor services, data connectors, monitoring, logging, evaluation tools, accessibility testing, and support infrastructure. Additional funding will be needed for content cleanup, policy development, employee training, communications, pilot incentives where appropriate, and independent security or privacy assessments. A contingency reserve should be maintained for usage growth, additional safeguards, integration complexity, and unanticipated remediation work.

The organization should also establish a permanent service-management model before the end of the implementation period. This model should define ownership for platform administration, data-source approval, access management, incident response, vendor management, user support, performance reporting, and periodic risk review.

## Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use

The assistant will operate under an enterprise AI governance framework that aligns with existing security, privacy, legal, records, procurement, accessibility, and information-management requirements. All connected data sources will be reviewed for authorization, quality, sensitivity, ownership, and retention requirements. The assistant will enforce existing user permissions rather than create broader access to information.

Employees will receive clear guidance stating that AI outputs may be incomplete, inaccurate, outdated, biased, or inappropriate for a particular context. Users must verify material facts, protect confidential information, cite or preserve source material where required, and obtain human approval before relying on outputs for consequential decisions or external communications.

The organization will maintain monitoring and reporting processes for inappropriate use, data leakage, harmful outputs, hallucinations, bias, system misuse, and security incidents. A documented escalation process will allow employees to report concerns and receive timely assistance. High-risk use cases will require additional review and may require specialized controls, independent validation, or exclusion from the service.

The program will also address accessibility and inclusion by testing the assistant with assistive technologies, supporting accessible content formats, and ensuring that adoption does not create barriers for employees who cannot or do not use the tool.

## Success Criteria

The deployment will be considered successful if it demonstrates measurable value while maintaining appropriate levels of trust, security, and control. Target measures will be finalized during the foundation phase, but the program should aim to achieve the following outcomes within the first twelve months:

- At least 60 percent of employees are aware of the assistant, and at least 40 percent use it monthly after full deployment.
- Participating users report meaningful time savings on prioritized tasks, with a target average reduction of at least 20 percent for selected use cases.
- At least 75 percent of active users report that the assistant improves their ability to find information, draft content, or complete routine work.
- Response quality, relevance, and source attribution meet agreed standards in formal evaluations, with documented improvement throughout the pilot and rollout.
- No material security or privacy incidents result from uncontrolled access, inappropriate configuration, or avoidable misuse.
- All employees receive baseline responsible-use guidance before or at the time of access, with role-specific training for higher-risk functions.
- Support volumes, service availability, response times, and operating costs remain within approved thresholds.
- Business units demonstrate documented examples of improved cycle time, reduced duplication, better knowledge access, or improved consistency.
- Governance controls, access reviews, incident procedures, and performance reporting are operating as a sustainable business service by the end of the first year.

Success will not be measured by usage alone. The organization will also assess whether employees are using the assistant for appropriate purposes, whether outputs are reliable enough to support work, whether information remains properly protected, and whether benefits are distributed fairly across departments and employee groups.

## Conclusion

Deploying an internal AI assistant across a 5,000-employee organization represents a significant opportunity to improve productivity, knowledge access, and consistency while establishing a disciplined foundation for future AI initiatives. A phased approach will allow the organization to demonstrate value quickly, learn from real-world use, address risks before they scale, and build employee confidence through training and transparency.

With executive sponsorship, cross-functional governance, responsible technical design, strong information management, and clear measurement, the organization can introduce an assistant that is useful in everyday work and trustworthy in the environments where accuracy, privacy, and accountability matter most. The proposed twelve-month program will deliver an initial enterprise capability while creating the operating model required for sustainable, responsible expansion.

## Objectives

The project will deliver a secure, reliable, and useful AI assistant that supports employees in their daily work. The primary objectives are to:

- Provide employees with conversational access to approved internal policies, procedures, knowledge bases, and resources.
- Reduce the time required to find information, draft routine content, summarize documents, and complete repetitive tasks.
- Improve consistency in the use of organizational policies and standard operating procedures.
- Integrate the assistant with selected productivity, collaboration, and enterprise systems.
- Establish clear governance for privacy, security, responsible use, data retention, model behavior, and human oversight.
- Build employee confidence and adoption through training, communications, and transparent operating practices.
- Create a scalable foundation for future AI-enabled workflows and business applications.

The assistant will augment employees rather than replace professional judgment or accountability. It will not independently make employment, legal, financial, safety, compliance, or other high-impact decisions.

## Scope

The project will cover the design, implementation, testing, deployment, and initial optimization of an internal AI assistant available to the organization’s 5,000 employees.

The initial release will include conversational question answering over approved internal content; document summarization; drafting and rewriting support; meeting and project assistance; policy and procedure guidance; and assistance with common workplace tasks. Responses will include links or references to source materials where feasible, and the assistant will clearly communicate uncertainty or limitations when it cannot provide a reliable answer.

The assistant will initially connect to selected, high-value information sources such as the intranet, approved document repositories, policy libraries, knowledge bases, and collaboration platforms. Integrations with business systems will be limited to low-risk, read-only or user-initiated functions during the first deployment phase. Any action that changes records, sends communications, approves transactions, or affects an employee or customer will require explicit user confirmation and appropriate authorization.

The project includes identity and access management, role-based permissions, data classification, audit logging, security testing, content governance, user training, support processes, and usage analytics. It also includes the development of an AI governance framework covering acceptable use, prohibited use, data handling, escalation, incident response, and periodic performance review.

The initial scope excludes autonomous decision-making, unrestricted access to all enterprise data, unsupervised external communications, automated personnel decisions, and high-risk operational actions. Additional capabilities may be considered after the organization demonstrates that the assistant meets defined security, reliability, adoption, and value thresholds.

## Delivery Approach and Timeline

The project is expected to run over approximately nine months, followed by an ongoing optimization period.

During the first month, the project team will establish governance, confirm executive sponsorship, define priority use cases, assess the organization’s data and technology environment, and establish baseline measures for productivity, employee experience, and support demand. Stakeholder workshops will identify the highest-value employee needs and determine which information sources are sufficiently accurate and governed for inclusion.

Months two and three will focus on solution design and preparation. The team will select the platform and implementation architecture, define security and access controls, prepare approved content sources, design the user experience, and establish evaluation methods. Legal, privacy, information security, records management, human resources, compliance, and employee representatives will review the proposed operating model. A limited prototype will be developed using representative content and test accounts.

Months four and five will comprise a controlled pilot involving approximately 250 to 500 employees from a representative set of business functions. Pilot users will receive training and guidance on appropriate use. The project team will evaluate answer quality, source accuracy, security behavior, usability, latency, accessibility, and the assistant’s ability to handle ambiguous or inappropriate requests. Feedback will be collected through surveys, interviews, usage analytics, and structured testing.

Months six and seven will support a broader readiness phase. Pilot findings will be incorporated into the solution, content quality issues will be addressed, support procedures will be finalized, and the assistant will be expanded to approximately 1,000 to 1,500 employees across additional functions. Communications and training materials will be refined, and operational teams will complete readiness reviews for security, privacy, service management, and business continuity.

Months eight and nine will deliver the organization-wide rollout to all 5,000 employees. Deployment will occur in managed waves to control demand on support teams and allow rapid remediation of issues. Employees will receive role-appropriate training, clear acceptable-use guidance, and access to help resources. Executive sponsors and business leaders will reinforce responsible adoption and identify additional use cases.

After the initial rollout, the organization will enter an ongoing optimization phase. Performance, adoption, user feedback, content quality, and risk indicators will be reviewed regularly. New integrations and use cases will be approved through the governance process and introduced only when their benefits and risks have been evaluated.

## Resource Requirements

The project will require executive sponsorship and a cross-functional delivery team. The core team should include a program director, product manager, enterprise architect, AI or machine-learning specialist, security architect, privacy and legal representatives, data and knowledge-management leads, integration engineers, user-experience and accessibility specialists, change-management and communications leads, training resources, service-management personnel, and business representatives from participating functions.

During implementation, the program is expected to require approximately 15 to 25 dedicated full-time-equivalent resources, supplemented by part-time subject-matter experts and representatives from business units. The exact level will depend on the selected platform, integration complexity, content readiness, and the degree of customization required.

Technology resources will include an enterprise AI platform or approved model service, secure hosting or cloud capacity, identity and access-management integration, document and knowledge connectors, monitoring and logging capabilities, data-loss-prevention controls, testing environments, and service-management tools. The solution should support encryption in transit and at rest, tenant isolation where applicable, configurable retention, administrative controls, auditability, and contractual commitments that organizational data will not be used to train public models without authorization.

The budget should cover platform licensing or consumption, implementation services, integration and data preparation, security and privacy assessments, accessibility testing, employee training, communications, support capacity, and ongoing model and content management. A contingency reserve should be maintained for additional data remediation, integration work, and scaling costs identified during the pilot.

Business units will be responsible for nominating content owners, validating high-value use cases, confirming the accuracy of information within their domains, and participating in testing. The central program team will own the platform, governance framework, deployment process, evaluation standards, and operational reporting.

## Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use

The assistant will operate under a formal governance model overseen by an executive steering committee and supported by an AI governance working group. The steering committee will provide strategic direction, approve major scope decisions, and resolve cross-functional issues. The working group will oversee use-case approval, risk classification, data access, model evaluation, incident management, and periodic policy updates.

Access to information will follow existing identity, role, and authorization rules. The assistant will not provide content to a user who could not access the underlying source through normal enterprise permissions. Sensitive information will be subject to additional controls, and restricted data sources will be excluded unless they have been specifically assessed and approved.

Employees will be instructed not to enter personal, highly sensitive, or regulated information into the assistant unless the relevant use case and platform controls explicitly permit it. The assistant’s outputs will be treated as drafts or guidance unless independently verified. Users will remain responsible for reviewing generated content and for decisions made using that content.

The organization will conduct predeployment and recurring testing for hallucinations, prompt injection, unauthorized disclosure, bias, inappropriate content, accessibility barriers, and inconsistent policy interpretation. A clear process will allow employees to report inaccurate, unsafe, biased, or inappropriate responses. Significant incidents will be investigated, documented, and escalated according to established risk and security procedures.

## Success Criteria

The project will be considered successful when the assistant is available to all 5,000 employees through approved channels, meets defined security and privacy requirements, and demonstrates measurable value in priority use cases.

Key success measures will include:

- At least 70 percent of employees completing or accessing introductory training within three months of organization-wide deployment.
- At least 50 percent of employees using the assistant within the first six months, with sustained monthly usage demonstrating continued value rather than one-time experimentation.
- A measurable reduction in time spent locating internal information and completing selected routine tasks, with a target of at least 20 percent improvement in priority workflows.
- User satisfaction of at least  sphinx 75 percent among active users, measured through recurring surveys and task-level feedback.
- At least 85 percent of evaluated responses meeting agreed standards for relevance, clarity, and factual grounding in approved use cases.
- No material unauthorized disclosure of restricted information and no unresolved critical security or privacy findings at launch.
- Successful completion of independent security, privacy, accessibility, and operational-readiness assessments.
- Documented ownership and quality-review processes for all major content sources connected to the assistant.
- A defined support model with service-level targets, incident procedures, usage monitoring, and regular governance reviews.
- A prioritized pipeline of future use cases supported by evidence from the pilot and first six months of production use.

Success will be evaluated not only by adoption volume but also by the quality, safety, and business value of usage. The program will be adjusted if employees cannot reliably find accurate information, if risk controls are ineffective, or if the assistant does not produce measurable improvements in targeted workflows.

## Conclusion

Deploying an internal AI assistant across the organization represents a practical opportunity to improve access to knowledge, reduce repetitive work, and strengthen the employee experience. A phased approach will allow the organization to realize benefits while managing security, privacy, accuracy, and adoption risks. By combining strong governance, reliable enterprise content, thoughtful integrations, employee education, and measurable outcomes, the organization can establish a trusted AI capability that delivers immediate value and provides a foundation for responsible innovation over time.

During months nine and ten, the service will expand to approximately 1,500 employees, including additional business units and higher-volume use cases. Integrations with selected support and knowledge workflows may be introduced during this stage, subject to separate security and process approvals. Additional training, communications, and manager toolkits will support adoption while maintaining realistic expectations about the assistant’s capabilities and limitations.

During months eleven and twelve, the assistant will be made available to the remaining employee population in controlled waves. Each wave will be monitored for reliability, security, user satisfaction, and support demand. At the conclusion of the rollout, the program will conduct a formal benefits review and produce a roadmap for the next phase, including additional content sources, workflow integrations, and potential expansion to approved advanced capabilities.

After the initial twelve-month program, the service will transition to a permanent product and operations model. Quarterly governance reviews will assess performance, risk, content quality, usage, and new use-case requests.

## Resource Requirements

The program will require executive sponsorship from a senior business leader and a cross-functional delivery team. Core staffing should include a program or product director, product manager, enterprise architect, AI or machine-learning engineers, application and integration engineers, data and knowledge engineers, user-experience and service-design specialists, security engineers, privacy and legal advisers, risk and compliance representatives, change-management and communications leads, training specialists, service-desk personnel, and business subject-matter experts.

A reasonable initial team is approximately 20 to 30 full-time equivalent employees, supplemented by part-time representatives from major business functions. The team should include dedicated content owners for each knowledge domain and a support model capable of handling user questions, suspected inaccuracies, access issues, and responsible-use concerns.

Technology resources will include an enterprise AI platform or approved model provider, secure hosting, identity and access management, document indexing and retrieval services, logging and monitoring, content-filtering and policy-enforcement capabilities, evaluation tools, analytics, backup and recovery, and integration services. The platform must support tenant isolation or equivalent enterprise protections, encryption in transit and at rest, configurable retention, administrative controls, auditability, and contractual commitments regarding organizational data.

The program budget should cover platform and model usage, implementation services, security testing, data preparation, integration work, training and communications, change management, service operations, and contingency. A preliminary first-year planning estimate is approximately $3 million to $6 million, depending on platform selection, integration complexity, licensing structure, usage volume, and the amount of internal staffing already available. Ongoing annual operating costs should be established after the pilot, using actual utilization and support data.

Business participation is essential. Each participating function will provide content owners, approve its information sources, define acceptable responses, nominate pilot users, and participate in benefits measurement. The organization will also designate an AI governance committee responsible for policy, risk decisions, exception handling, and prioritization of future use cases.

## Governance, Security, and Risk Management

The assistant will operate under a formal governance framework aligned with existing information-security, privacy, records-management, compliance, and acceptable-use policies. Access to knowledge will respect source-system permissions wherever technically feasible, and content will be classified before ingestion. The assistant will not be permitted to bypass existing authorization controls.

Responses will clearly distinguish generated content from authoritative source material and will provide citations or links when the system relies on internal documentation. Users will be informed that responses may be incomplete or incorrect and that they remain responsible for validating outputs before making consequential decisions or sharing them externally.

The organization will maintain audit logs covering authentication, source access, administrative changes, selected prompts and responses where legally and operationally appropriate, system events, and actions taken through integrations. Monitoring will identify abnormal usage, potential data leakage, harmful content, repeated quality failures, and attempts to manipulate system behavior. Sensitive data handling will be governed by retention, masking, access, and deletion requirements.

A documented incident-response process will address inaccurate or harmful responses, exposure of restricted information, unauthorized actions, model or platform outages, and security attacks. Each major knowledge domain will have a content owner responsible for correcting outdated or misleading information. The program will also establish a process for employee feedback, appeal, escalation, and reporting of inappropriate outputs.

## Success Criteria

The deployment will be considered successful when the assistant is securely available to the intended employee population, operates within approved governance controls, and demonstrates measurable value in priority use cases.

By the end of the first year, the program should achieve active usage by at least 60 percent of employees, with at least 40 percent using the service monthly after the initial adoption period. In the pilot and early expansion phases, at least 80 percent of evaluated responses for approved knowledge use cases should be judged materially useful, with source attribution available for the great majority of factual answers. Critical access-control, privacy, and data-leakage findings must be resolved before broad deployment, and no high-severity incident should remain without a documented remediation plan.

The service should reduce average time spent locating approved information by at least 25 percent in the initial target domains and reduce avoidable routine support requests by at least 10 percent where the assistant is positioned as a first point of assistance. User surveys should show improved employee confidence in finding information and completing selected tasks, while employee trust measures should remain stable or improve. The service should meet agreed availability and performance targets, with operating costs tracked against usage and realized benefits.

Success will also be measured by organizational readiness. Each onboarded knowledge domain must have an accountable owner, review schedule, access policy, and quality baseline. All employees must receive clear guidance on acceptable use, data handling, and human review. The organization must have a functioning governance process for approving new use cases, assessing risks, managing incidents, and retiring low-value or unsafe capabilities.

## Conclusion

Deploying an internal AI assistant across 5,000 employees is a strategic capability program rather than a stand-alone technology implementation. A phased approach will allow the organization to demonstrate value quickly while building the security, governance, content ownership, and operational discipline required for sustainable adoption. By focusing first on high-value, well-governed use cases and expanding only when evidence supports doing so, the organization can improve employee productivity and access to knowledge while maintaining appropriate control over confidential information and consequential business decisions.

Approval of this proposal will authorize the twelve-month implementation program, establishment of the cross-functional delivery team, completion of platform and security assessments, and launch of a controlled pilot. The resulting service will provide a foundation for broader, responsible use of AI across the organization.

# Project Proposal: Enterprise Deployment of an Internal AI Assistant

## Background

Organizations across every industry are adopting artificial intelligence to improve productivity, accelerate decision-making, and make institutional knowledge easier to access. A 5,000-employee organization has significant opportunities to use an internal AI assistant to help employees find information, draft and summarize content, analyze data, automate routine work, and navigate internal processes.

At the same time, enterprise deployment requires careful attention to security, privacy, governance, accuracy, user adoption, and integration with existing systems. An unmanaged rollout could expose sensitive information, produce unreliable outputs, create compliance risks, or lead to fragmented use of unsupported tools. A centrally governed internal AI assistant will provide employees with a secure and consistent experience while enabling the organization to realize measurable business value.

This proposal recommends a phased deployment of an internal AI assistant for employees across the organization. The assistant will be accessible through approved enterprise channels and will use permission-aware connections to selected internal knowledge sources and business applications. The program will combine technology implementation with policy development, employee training, change management, and continuous performance monitoring.

## Objectives

The primary objective is to provide employees with a secure, reliable, and easy-to-use AI assistant that improves productivity without compromising organizational data or regulatory obligations.

The program will pursue the following objectives:

- Enable employees to quickly search, understand, summarize, and draft information using natural-language interaction.
- Reduce time spent on routine administrative and knowledge-management tasks.
- Improve access to approved internal policies, procedures, guidance, and institutional knowledge.
- Support departments in developing responsible, high-value AI use cases.
- Establish enterprise standards for security, privacy, acceptable use, human oversight, and accountability.
- Integrate the assistant with selected internal systems while preserving existing access controls.
- Create a scalable foundation for future AI-enabled automation and analytical capabilities.
- Measure business value, user adoption, output quality, and risk throughout the deployment.

The assistant will augment employee capabilities rather than replace professional judgment. Employees will remain responsible for reviewing outputs, validating important information, and making decisions within their roles.

## Scope

The initial deployment will cover all 5,000 employees, with access introduced through a phased rollout. The first release will focus on broadly useful capabilities that present manageable risk and can be supported consistently across the organization.

Core capabilities will include conversational question answering, document summarization, drafting and editing, translation, meeting and task support, structured information extraction, brainstorming, and assistance with approved internal content. The assistant will be configured to identify relevant sources where possible and will clearly communicate limitations when it cannot verify an answer.

The solution will connect initially to selected, high-quality knowledge repositories, such as approved policy libraries, employee guidance, process documentation, frequently asked questions, and other authoritative internal content. Additional integrations may include collaboration platforms, document-management systems, service-management tools, and productivity applications, subject to security and access-control reviews.

The project will include:

- Selection or configuration of an enterprise AI platform.
- Identity and access management integration, including single sign-on and role-based permissions.
- Secure retrieval of approved internal information.
- Data classification, retention, logging, and monitoring controls.
- Development of an enterprise AI policy and acceptable-use standards.
- Creation of a governance structure for use-case approval, risk review, and incident response.
- Pilot testing with representative business units.
- Organization-wide deployment and employee onboarding.
- Training for employees, managers, administrators, content owners, and support teams.
- Measurement of adoption, productivity, quality, satisfaction, and risk indicators.
- Establishment of an operating model for ongoing improvement.

The initial scope will exclude fully autonomous decision-making, unrestricted access to sensitive systems, automated actions that materially affect employees or customers, and use cases requiring the assistant to make final legal, financial, medical, employment, or safety-critical decisions. Such capabilities may be considered later through separate risk assessments and approval processes.

## Delivery Approach and Timeline

The project is expected to take approximately nine months from initiation to organization-wide deployment, followed by an ongoing optimization period.

During the first month, the organization will establish project governance, confirm executive sponsorship, define the target operating model, assess current technology and data environments, and identify priority use cases. Stakeholders from information technology, information security, legal, privacy, human resources, communications, procurement, records management, and representative business functions will participate in this phase.

Months two and three will focus on solution design and preparation. The project team will evaluate platform options, define the technical architecture, configure identity and access controls, classify initial data sources, establish logging and monitoring requirements, and draft enterprise policies and standards. Priority knowledge repositories will be prepared for use, including content cleanup, ownership assignment, metadata review, and access validation.

During months four and five, the team will build and test the initial solution. Testing will cover functionality, security, privacy, access control, data leakage, performance, usability, accessibility, and output quality. A controlled pilot will be launched with approximately 250 to 400 employees representing different roles, locations, technical skill levels, and risk profiles. Pilot participants will receive structured training and will be asked to provide feedback through surveys, interviews, and usage analytics.

Months six and seven will be dedicated to pilot evaluation and refinement. The organization will review usage patterns, quality issues, employee feedback, support demand, and identified risks. The assistant’s knowledge sources, prompts, policies, training materials, and support procedures will be updated. High-value use cases demonstrated during the pilot will be documented and converted into reusable guidance for broader deployment.

During months eight and nine, the assistant will be rolled out in waves to the full workforce. Deployment communications will explain the assistant’s capabilities, limitations, approved uses, and employee responsibilities. Department leaders and designated champions will support adoption, while help-desk and technical support teams will manage user assistance and incident escalation.

After the initial rollout, the program will enter an ongoing optimization phase. The organization will review performance and risk metrics at least quarterly, expand integrations only after appropriate review, refresh training and guidance, improve internal content quality, and retire or modify capabilities that do not meet expected standards.

## Resource Requirements

The program will require executive sponsorship, cross-functional participation, technical implementation capacity, and sustained operational ownership.

A recommended core team will include a program sponsor, program manager, product owner, enterprise architect, AI or machine-learning specialist, security architect, privacy or legal advisor, data governance lead, content and knowledge-management lead, change-management lead, training lead, communications specialist, user-experience designer, business analysts, quality-assurance specialists, and representatives from the service desk and business units. Some roles may be assigned part time or provided through existing teams, while others may require new capabilities or external support.

During implementation, the organization should plan for approximately 12 to 18 full-time-equivalent contributors across the core project team and participating functions, supplemented by subject-matter experts from departments. Ongoing operations will likely require a smaller permanent team, typically including a product owner, platform administrator, AI governance lead, security and privacy support, knowledge-management resources, analytics support, and service-desk capacity.

Technical resources will include an approved enterprise AI platform, secure cloud or on-premises hosting as appropriate, identity and access management, data-loss-prevention controls, audit logging, monitoring, content-indexing or retrieval services, application programming interfaces for approved integrations, and analytics for usage and performance measurement. The organization will also need development, testing, and production environments with appropriate separation and access controls.

Financial requirements will include platform licensing or consumption costs, implementation and integration services, security and privacy assessments, content preparation, employee training, communications, support-model development, and ongoing administration. A detailed budget should be finalized after platform selection and integration requirements are confirmed. The budget should also include contingency funding for data remediation, additional security controls, and changes identified during the pilot.

Business-unit participation is essential. Each department should designate a business owner and, where appropriate, an AI champion to identify use cases, validate content, encourage responsible adoption, and communicate feedback to the central program team. Content owners will be accountable for the accuracy, currency, and permissions of the information made available to the assistant.

## Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use

The assistant will operate under an enterprise governance framework approved before the pilot begins. The framework will define permitted and prohibited uses, data-handling requirements, human-review expectations, records-management obligations, accessibility standards, and procedures for reporting incidents or harmful outputs.

The solution will enforce existing identity and access permissions wherever it retrieves internal information. Users will not receive access to content or systems they could not otherwise access. Sensitive data will be handled according to existing classification and privacy requirements, and the organization will establish clear rules for entering confidential, personal, regulated, or third-party information into the assistant.

The program will include pre-deployment testing and ongoing monitoring for inaccurate responses, unauthorized disclosure, bias, inappropriate content, prompt manipulation, system misuse, and service degradation. High-impact use cases will require additional review and documented human oversight. Employees will be informed that AI-generated content may contain errors and must be reviewed before it is used in external communications, formal decisions, regulated processes, or other consequential activities.

A cross-functional AI Governance Committee will oversee policy, risk acceptance, use-case approval, performance reviews, and significant changes to the service. The committee will receive regular reports from the product and security teams and will have authority to pause or restrict capabilities when risks exceed approved thresholds.

## Success Criteria

The project will be considered successful when the assistant is available to the intended employee population, operates within approved security and governance controls, and demonstrates measurable value in priority use cases.

Initial success measures will include:

- At least 90 percent of employees provisioned with access by the end of the rollout.
- At least 60 percent of employees actively using the assistant within six months of general availability.
- User satisfaction of at least 75 percent among active users.
- At least 80 percent of pilot participants reporting that the assistant saves time or improves the quality of their work.
- Demonstrated time savings of 20 percent or more in selected priority workflows.
- A measurable reduction in time required to locate approved internal information.
- Successful completion of security, privacy, accessibility, and performance testing before general availability.
- No material unauthorized disclosure of confidential or personal information.
- Documented ownership and review schedules for all connected knowledge sources.
- Support volumes that remain within agreed service levels after the initial adoption period.
- Completion of mandatory training for all employees before or shortly after access is provided.
- A documented pipeline of validated use cases for future expansion.

Success will not be measured by usage alone. The organization will evaluate whether employees are using the assistant appropriately, whether outputs are accurate enough for their intended purposes, whether business processes are improving, and whether risks are being identified and managed effectively. Results will be reported to executive leadership quarterly, with recommendations for investment, modification, expansion, or restriction.

## Conclusion

Deploying an internal AI assistant across a 5,000-employee organization represents a significant opportunity to improve productivity, knowledge access, and employee experience. The greatest value will come from treating the initiative as an enterprise transformation program rather than a technology installation. A phased rollout, strong governance, secure architecture, high-quality internal content, practical training, and rigorous measurement will allow the organization to capture benefits while managing operational and reputational risk.

Approval of this proposal will authorize the organization to begin detailed planning, platform evaluation, stakeholder engagement, and preparation for a controlled pilot. The resulting program will provide employees with a trusted foundation for responsible AI use and position the organization to expand its capabilities as technology, business needs, and governance practices mature.

# Proposal: Deployment of an Internal AI Assistant Across the Organization

## Background

The organization’s employees spend significant time searching for information, interpreting internal policies, drafting routine communications, preparing reports, and navigating multiple business systems. Knowledge is distributed across document repositories, intranets, collaboration platforms, shared drives, and specialized applications, making it difficult for employees to locate accurate information quickly. These challenges create duplicated effort, slow decision-making, and inconsistent access to organizational knowledge.

Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence make it possible to provide employees with a secure, conversational interface to approved internal information and productivity tools. An internal AI assistant could help employees find policies and procedures, summarize documents, draft content, answer questions about approved organizational resources, and automate selected low-risk tasks. Deployed responsibly, the assistant would increase productivity while preserving existing access controls, protecting confidential information, and maintaining human accountability for business decisions.

This proposal recommends the phased deployment of an internal AI assistant for the organization’s approximately 5,000 employees. The program will begin with targeted use cases and controlled pilots, followed by progressive expansion based on measurable outcomes, user feedback, security validation, and operational readiness.

## Objectives

The primary objective is to provide employees with a reliable, secure, and easy-to-use AI assistant that improves access to information and reduces time spent on repetitive knowledge work.

The program will pursue the following objectives:

- Enable employees to search, summarize, and interact with approved internal knowledge using natural-language prompts.
- Reduce the time required to locate policies, procedures, templates, and other frequently used resources.
- Support drafting, summarization, translation, meeting preparation, and other low-risk productivity activities.
- Improve consistency by grounding responses in authoritative organizational content and linking users to source materials.
- Establish clear governance for privacy, security, data retention, acceptable use, human oversight, and model performance.
- Integrate the assistant with selected collaboration, document-management, and business systems where the value and risk profile justify integration.
- Create a scalable foundation for future AI-enabled workflows while maintaining appropriate controls over sensitive information and automated actions.

## Scope

The initial deployment will cover all 5,000 employees, with access and capabilities introduced in phases. The first release will focus on a secure conversational assistant capable of answering questions from approved internal documents, identifying relevant sources, summarizing content, and assisting with common writing and analysis tasks. Users will be informed when they are interacting with AI and will be expected to review outputs before relying on them.

Priority use cases will include employee self-service, policy and procedure discovery, internal communications, document summarization, meeting preparation, knowledge transfer, and drafting of routine materials. Business units may propose additional use cases through a controlled intake and review process.

The assistant will connect initially to selected authoritative sources, such as the corporate intranet, approved policy libraries, knowledge bases, and document repositories. Integrations with email, collaboration tools, customer systems, financial systems, human resources platforms, or other transactional applications will be considered only after separate security, privacy, legal, and operational assessments. The initial phase will not authorize the assistant to make autonomous employment, financial, legal, safety, or customer-impacting decisions, nor will it permit unrestricted access to confidential systems.

The deployment will include identity-based authentication, role- and permission-aware retrieval, encryption, audit logging, data-loss prevention controls, usage monitoring, content governance, incident response procedures, and mechanisms for users to report inaccurate or unsafe responses. The program will also include employee training, communications, administrator enablement, and ongoing evaluation of answer quality and business value.

## Delivery Approach and Timeline

The program is expected to run over approximately nine months from approval to organization-wide availability, followed by continuous improvement.

During **months one and two**, the organization will establish the program foundation. This phase will confirm executive sponsorship, appoint a product owner, define governance, document approved and prohibited use cases, assess legal and regulatory requirements, select the technology approach, and establish security and privacy controls. The team will inventory and classify candidate knowledge sources, identify content owners, define success metrics, and prepare an initial implementation plan.

During **months three and four**, the organization will build and validate the minimum viable product. The assistant will be configured with approved internal content, integrated with enterprise identity and access management, and connected to a limited set of authoritative repositories. Testing will cover response accuracy, source attribution, access-control enforcement, data leakage, prompt injection, availability, performance, and user experience. A representative group of approximately 100 to 200 employees from different functions will participate in structured testing.

During **months five and six**, the organization will conduct a controlled pilot with approximately 500 employees. Pilot participants will receive role-specific training and guidance on appropriate use. The project team will monitor adoption, task completion, response quality, support demand, security events, and user feedback. Content gaps and technical issues will be addressed before expansion. Pilot results will be reviewed by the steering committee, which will approve, modify, or pause the next phase based on predefined readiness criteria.

During **months seven and eight**, the assistant will be expanded to approximately 2,000 employees across the organization. Additional approved knowledge sources and selected low-risk integrations may be introduced during this phase. Communications, training, service-desk support, and business-unit champions will be scaled to support adoption. Performance and risk reviews will continue at regular intervals.

During **month nine**, the organization will complete the broader rollout to all 5,000 employees, subject to successful completion of security, privacy, operational, and user-readiness reviews. The launch will be accompanied by enterprise communications, mandatory baseline training, published acceptable-use guidance, and an established support and governance model. After launch, the assistant will enter a continuous-improvement phase involving quarterly performance reviews, content maintenance, model and vendor assessments, and prioritization of new use cases.

## Resource Requirements

The program will require executive sponsorship and a cross-functional team with responsibility for product management, technology delivery, information security, privacy, legal and compliance, enterprise architecture, data governance, communications, training, and support.

A core implementation team of approximately 12 to 18 full-time equivalent staff is anticipated during deployment. This team should include a program or product lead; solution and enterprise architects; AI or machine-learning engineers; software and integration engineers; information-security specialists; data and content-governance leads; user-experience and change-management professionals; testing and quality-assurance specialists; and technical writers or training designers. Representatives from human resources, legal, risk, internal audit, records management, and major business functions should participate through a governance group or allocated part-time capacity.

The organization will need a secure AI platform or approved enterprise AI service, identity and access-management integration, document and knowledge connectors, monitoring and analytics capabilities, content-filtering and data-loss prevention controls, logging and audit infrastructure, and service-desk integration. Technology selection should account for data residency, contractual protections, model-training policies, interoperability, scalability, availability, accessibility, and total cost of ownership.

A preliminary budget should account for platform licensing or consumption costs, implementation and integration services, security and privacy assessments, content remediation, employee training, communications, technical support, ongoing administration, and evaluation. Depending on the selected architecture and degree of integration, first-year costs are expected to be driven less by employee access alone than by content preparation, governance, integration complexity, and support requirements. A formal business case and vendor assessment should establish the final budget before implementation begins.

Content owners will be responsible for ensuring that information made available to the assistant is current, accurate, appropriately classified, and governed according to existing records-management requirements. Business units will also provide subject-matter experts to validate responses and identify high-value use cases.

## Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use

The assistant will operate under a formal governance framework approved before pilot launch. The framework will define acceptable and prohibited uses, data-handling requirements, review obligations, escalation procedures, retention rules, model and vendor oversight, and accountability for business outcomes.

The assistant will respect existing user permissions and will not provide information that a user is not authorized to access. Responses should cite or link to source documents wherever feasible, and users will be reminded that AI-generated content may be incomplete or inaccurate. Human review will remain mandatory for decisions or communications involving legal, financial, employment, safety, regulatory, security, or other material consequences.

Security testing will address unauthorized access, sensitive-data exposure, malicious prompts, unsafe tool use, inaccurate retrieval, and model behavior under adversarial conditions. The organization will maintain an incident-management process for suspected data leakage, harmful output, system misuse, or material performance failures. Access may be restricted or suspended for users, data sources, or use cases that introduce unacceptable risk.

## Success Criteria

The program will be considered successful when the assistant demonstrates measurable value without compromising security, privacy, compliance, or employee trust. Key success criteria will include:

- At least 60 percent of eligible employees actively using the assistant within six months of organization-wide launch.
- A measurable reduction in the time employees spend locating approved policies, procedures, and internal knowledge, with a target of at least 25 percent for priority tasks.
- At least 70 percent of surveyed users reporting that the assistant improves their productivity or ability to find information.
- At least 85 percent of evaluated responses for priority knowledge use cases judged accurate, relevant, and appropriately sourced.
- No material unauthorized disclosure of confidential or restricted information during testing, pilot, or production use.
- Completion of required security, privacy, legal, accessibility, and compliance reviews before each expansion phase.
- Demonstrated adherence to role-based access controls and audit requirements across all connected repositories.
- A defined and sustainable process for content ownership, issue resolution, model monitoring, user support, and periodic risk review.
- Documented productivity or service improvements in at least three high-value business processes.
- Positive user sentiment and declining support demand after the initial adoption period.

Success will be assessed through platform analytics, controlled task testing, user surveys, help-desk data, security monitoring, content-quality reviews, and business-unit outcome measurements. The steering committee will review results at the end of each deployment phase and will retain authority to modify scope, delay expansion, or discontinue specific capabilities if the benefits do not justify the risks.

## Conclusion

Deploying an internal AI assistant across a 5,000-employee organization represents an opportunity to improve productivity, strengthen access to institutional knowledge, and establish a disciplined foundation for broader digital transformation. A phased approach will allow the organization to demonstrate value quickly while validating security, privacy, content quality, user adoption, and operational readiness before scaling.

Approval of this proposal will authorize the discovery and foundation phase, including detailed architecture, governance design, business-case development, vendor evaluation, and pilot preparation. The organization should proceed with the expectation that responsible AI adoption is an ongoing capability rather than a one-time technology implementation. With appropriate investment, oversight, and employee engagement, the assistant can become a trusted internal service that helps employees work more efficiently while preserving human judgment and organizational accountability.

# Proposal: Deployment of an Internal AI Assistant Across the Organization

## Background

The organization’s 5,000 employees rely on a growing volume of policies, procedures, operational documents, technical resources, project records, and institutional knowledge. Finding accurate information often requires searching across multiple systems, contacting subject-matter experts, or repeating work that has already been completed elsewhere. These inefficiencies increase administrative effort, slow decision-making, create inconsistent responses, and make it more difficult for employees to access the knowledge they need to perform effectively.

Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence make it possible to provide employees with a secure, conversational interface for accessing approved organizational knowledge and completing routine knowledge-work tasks. An internal AI assistant could help employees locate policies, summarize documents, draft communications, answer questions about internal processes, generate first drafts, and direct users to authoritative systems and experts. Properly designed, the assistant would augment—not replace—employees and existing business applications.

This proposal recommends a phased deployment of an internal AI assistant for the organization’s 5,000 employees. The solution would be delivered through approved enterprise channels, governed by the organization’s security and privacy requirements, and integrated with authoritative internal information sources. The initial implementation would focus on high-value, low-risk use cases, followed by measured expansion based on user adoption, quality, and business impact.

## Objectives

The project will establish a secure, reliable, and scalable internal AI assistant that improves access to organizational knowledge and reduces the time employees spend on repetitive information-related tasks.

The primary objectives are to:

- Provide employees with a single, conversational entry point to approved internal knowledge.
- Improve the speed and consistency of answers about policies, procedures, services, and organizational processes.
- Reduce time spent searching for information, drafting routine content, and responding to recurring questions.
- Enable employees to summarize, compare, classify, and transform approved documents and information.
- Preserve existing access controls so that employees receive only information they are authorized to access.
- Establish clear standards for responsible AI use, including privacy, security, transparency, human oversight, and content ownership.
- Create a reusable platform and operating model that can support future AI-enabled capabilities.

The assistant will be positioned as a productivity and knowledge-access tool. It will not make autonomous employment, legal, financial, safety, or other high-impact decisions, and it will not replace required professional review or established approval processes.

## Scope

The initial scope includes the design, configuration, testing, deployment, and operational support of an enterprise AI assistant available to all employees, with a controlled pilot preceding organization-wide release.

The assistant will initially support general enterprise use cases such as answering questions about approved policies and procedures, locating relevant documents, summarizing internal materials, drafting routine emails and reports, converting content into different formats, preparing meeting summaries from authorized inputs, and directing employees to the correct service desk, system, or subject-matter expert. Selected departments may also pilot more specialized capabilities, such as human resources policy navigation, information technology support, procurement guidance, finance process assistance, and customer or operational knowledge retrieval.

The solution will connect to selected authoritative sources, which may include the intranet, document-management repositories, knowledge bases, policy libraries, service-management platforms, and other approved systems. Each source will undergo a readiness assessment covering ownership, data quality, currency, permissions, and suitability for AI retrieval. Content that is obsolete, duplicated, poorly governed, or improperly classified will not be included until remediation is complete.

The project includes identity and access management, role-based access controls, audit logging, usage monitoring, response-quality evaluation, data-loss prevention controls, user training, communications, support processes, and an AI governance framework. It also includes the establishment of procedures for reporting inaccurate or harmful responses and for removing or correcting source content.

The initial scope excludes fully autonomous actions in business systems, unsupervised external communications, use of confidential information in unapproved models, and automated decisions that could materially affect employees, customers, vendors, or organizational risk. Any future expansion into these areas will require separate assessment and approval.

## Delivery Approach and Timeline

The project is expected to run over approximately nine months, followed by continuous improvement and operational scaling.

During the first month, the project team will establish governance, confirm executive sponsorship, define priority use cases, identify business and technical owners, and complete an initial assessment of information sources, security requirements, privacy considerations, and regulatory obligations. The organization will also define baseline measures for search time, service-desk demand, employee satisfaction, and other relevant performance indicators.

During months two and three, the team will select and configure the technology platform, establish the target architecture, integrate enterprise identity services, and prepare the first set of approved knowledge sources. Security, privacy, legal, records-management, and risk stakeholders will review the proposed design. The team will also develop response standards, acceptable-use guidance, evaluation methods, and escalation procedures.

During months four and five, the assistant will be developed and tested in a controlled environment. Testing will cover factual accuracy, source attribution, access-control enforcement, prompt-injection resistance, privacy protection, availability, usability, and performance. A representative test set will be created from real organizational questions, with results reviewed by designated subject-matter experts. Critical defects will be resolved before pilot release.

During month six, the organization will conduct a pilot with approximately 300 to 500 employees representing different departments, roles, technical abilities, and information needs. Pilot participants will receive training and structured guidance. Their feedback, usage patterns, quality ratings, and support issues will be used to improve the assistant, refine source content, and confirm operational readiness.

During months seven and eight, the assistant will be expanded in waves to the remaining workforce. Deployment communications, role-specific training, manager toolkits, office hours, and support resources will accompany each wave. High-volume departments and teams with strong use cases will be prioritized, while access to higher-risk capabilities will remain controlled.

During month nine, the project will transition to business-as-usual operations. The team will complete a formal benefits review, confirm ownership and service-level expectations, document lessons learned, and approve a roadmap for additional integrations and use cases. Thereafter, the assistant will be managed through a regular cycle of content review, model and security evaluation, user feedback analysis, and capability improvement.

## Resource Requirements

The project will require executive sponsorship, cross-functional governance, technical implementation capacity, business participation, and sustained operational ownership.

A core delivery team should include a program manager, product owner, enterprise architect, AI or machine-learning engineer, integration engineers, data and content specialists, cybersecurity and privacy representatives, user-experience support, change-management and communications leads, training resources, and service-desk representatives. Subject-matter experts from human resources, information technology, finance, legal, procurement, operations, and other priority functions will contribute to use-case definition, content validation, testing, and adoption activities.

After deployment, the organization should establish a permanent operating team responsible for platform administration, content and knowledge governance, security monitoring, quality evaluation, vendor management, user support, and continuous improvement. Business units should designate content owners accountable for the accuracy, currency, and accessibility of information made available to the assistant.

Technology resources will include an enterprise AI platform or approved model service, secure hosting, identity and access management, content connectors, retrieval and indexing services, monitoring and analytics, data-loss prevention, audit logging, and integration with existing collaboration or intranet channels. The selected platform must support enterprise data protections, contractual controls over data usage, configurable retention, administrative oversight, and the ability to enforce source-level permissions.

The budget will include software or consumption licensing, implementation services, integration and data-preparation work, security and privacy assessment, training and communications, pilot support, and ongoing operations. A contingency should be reserved for source-system remediation, additional security controls, unexpected integration complexity, and changes in licensing or usage demand. Final funding should be approved after the discovery phase produces a confirmed implementation design and total-cost estimate.

## Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use

The assistant will operate under a formal governance framework overseen by a cross-functional steering group. The framework will define permitted and prohibited use cases, data classifications, approval requirements, human-review expectations, model and vendor oversight, incident response, records handling, and procedures for evaluating new capabilities.

Employees will be informed when they are interacting with AI-generated content and will receive clear guidance that responses may be incomplete or incorrect. The assistant will provide links or citations to the internal sources used to generate an answer whenever technically possible. Users will be encouraged to verify important information and remain accountable for decisions and communications produced with AI assistance.

Security controls will include single sign-on, role- and attribute-based access enforcement, encryption, environment segregation, logging, monitoring, prompt-injection defenses, restricted administrative access, and testing against data-exfiltration scenarios. Sensitive information will be handled according to existing classification and retention policies. The system will not use organizational data to train external models unless explicitly approved through the organization’s governance and contracting processes.

## Success Criteria

The deployment will be considered successful when it demonstrates measurable employee value without compromising security, privacy, or trust.

Within six months of organization-wide launch, the program should achieve participation from at least 60 percent of employees, with at least 35 percent using the assistant monthly. At least 70 percent of active users should report that the assistant helps them complete work more quickly or find information more easily. The organization should target a 20 percent reduction in time spent answering common internal information requests and a 15 percent reduction in avoidable, repetitive service-desk or support inquiries in participating functions.

For answer quality, at least 85 percent of evaluated responses should be rated factually useful and appropriately grounded in approved sources, with critical-use-case accuracy targets set higher where necessary. The assistant should provide source references for at least 90 percent of knowledge-based responses where citations are applicable. Access-control testing must demonstrate that users cannot retrieve information beyond their existing permissions, and no material privacy or security incident should result from the deployment.

Operationally, the service should meet agreed availability and response-time targets, establish documented ownership for all connected knowledge sources, and resolve reported content or safety issues within defined service levels. The organization should also demonstrate that employees have completed required training and that managers understand appropriate use, limitations, and escalation procedures.

The program will use these measures, together with employee feedback, business-unit outcomes, support volumes, and total cost of ownership, to determine whether to expand integrations and introduce more specialized AI capabilities. By combining a focused initial scope with strong governance and continuous measurement, the organization can provide meaningful productivity benefits while building the confidence, controls, and operational foundation required for responsible enterprise-wide AI adoption.

It will operate within the organization’s existing identity, security, compliance, and information-management frameworks and will provide responses grounded in approved internal content wherever possible.

## Objectives

The project will establish a trusted internal AI capability that delivers measurable value while protecting organizational information and maintaining appropriate human oversight. Its primary objectives are to:

- Improve employees’ ability to find, understand, and apply internal information.
- Reduce time spent on repetitive research, drafting, summarization, and knowledge-navigation tasks.
- Increase consistency in the use of policies, procedures, standards, and approved organizational guidance.
- Provide employees with a secure alternative to using unapproved public AI tools for internal work.

- Create a scalable platform and operating model that can support future AI-enabled business applications.
- Develop employee capability and confidence through training, practical guidance, and responsible-use education.

## Proposed Solution

The organization will deploy a centrally managed internal AI assistant accessible through the employee collaboration environment and web or mobile interfaces where appropriate. Employees will authenticate using the organization’s existing identity and access-management platform, with access governed by their existing permissions and role-based controls.

The assistant’s initial capabilities will include conversational question answering over approved internal knowledge sources, document summarization, drafting and editing, meeting and content summarization, translation where appropriate, structured information extraction, and assistance with routine business communications. Responses will include citations or links to source materials when the assistant is using internal knowledge, enabling employees to verify information and supporting accountability.
