# Proposal: Enterprise Deployment of an Internal AI Assistant

## Background

The organization’s 5,000 employees rely on a growing volume of policies, procedures, operational documents, applications, and institutional knowledge to perform their work. Much of this information is distributed across intranets, document repositories, collaboration platforms, shared drives, and specialized business systems. Employees often spend significant time searching for information, recreating existing content, drafting routine communications, and seeking assistance from subject-matter experts.

At the same time, employees are increasingly using publicly available generative AI tools. While these tools can improve productivity, their use may expose confidential information, create inconsistent outputs, and introduce privacy, security, compliance, and intellectual-property risks. A centrally managed internal AI assistant would provide employees with a secure and governed way to use AI while improving access to organizational knowledge and reducing repetitive work.

This proposal recommends the phased deployment of an internal AI assistant for the full organization. The assistant would provide conversational access to approved internal information, support common productivity tasks, and integrate with selected enterprise systems. The solution would be designed around the organization’s existing identity, security, privacy, records-management, and data-governance requirements.

## Objectives

The project will establish a trusted internal AI capability that improves employee productivity without compromising organizational data or decision-making standards. The primary objectives are to:

- Provide employees with secure, intuitive access to approved organizational knowledge through natural-language interaction.
- Reduce the time employees spend searching for information, interpreting policies, and completing routine drafting and summarization tasks.
- Improve consistency in the use of policies, procedures, templates, and approved guidance.
- Establish clear governance for AI use, including access controls, data protection, human oversight, auditability, and acceptable-use standards.
- Enable business units to identify and implement high-value AI use cases through a common enterprise platform.
- Build employee capability and confidence through training, communications, and practical guidance.
- Create a scalable foundation for future AI-enabled workflows and integrations.

The assistant will support employees in their work but will not replace professional judgment, managerial accountability, or formal approval processes. It will be positioned as a productivity and knowledge-support tool rather than an autonomous decision-maker.

## Scope

The project will select, configure, secure, test, and deploy an enterprise AI assistant accessible to all 5,000 employees through approved corporate channels. The initial solution will use the organization’s identity provider and existing role-based access controls so that employees can retrieve only the information they are authorized to access. Where feasible, the assistant will preserve the permissions applied in the source systems.

The initial release will focus on high-value, lower-risk use cases, including policy and procedure questions, internal knowledge search, document summarization, meeting and briefing preparation, drafting routine communications, creation of first-pass reports, and assistance with approved templates and workflows. Business units will be able to nominate additional use cases, which will be evaluated against value, risk, data readiness, and implementation complexity.

The project will include integration with selected enterprise content repositories and collaboration platforms, such as the corporate intranet, document-management systems, approved knowledge bases, and productivity applications. Integrations with sensitive systems, including human resources, legal, finance, customer, and regulated data environments, will be introduced only after separate security, privacy, and data-quality reviews.

The program will also establish an enterprise AI governance framework. This will include acceptable-use standards, data-classification requirements, model and vendor risk reviews, human-review expectations, incident reporting, records-management guidance, content ownership, performance monitoring, and a process for approving new use cases. The framework will define circumstances in which AI-generated content may be used directly and circumstances in which it must be reviewed or independently verified.

The initial deployment will not include autonomous actions that make employment, financial, legal, safety, or customer-impacting decisions. It will not permit unrestricted access to confidential information, bypass existing authorization controls, or replace formal systems of record. High-risk use cases will require additional review and approval before implementation.

## Delivery Approach and Timeline

The deployment will be delivered over approximately nine months in five phases.

During the first month, the project team will confirm executive sponsorship, establish governance, define the target operating model, document priority use cases, and assess the organization’s data, identity, security, privacy, and integration landscape. The team will also establish baseline measures for productivity, search effectiveness, employee satisfaction, and support demand.

During months two and three, the organization will evaluate and select the AI assistant platform. This phase will include technical due diligence, vendor and contract review, security and privacy assessment, architecture design, data-source prioritization, and development of the acceptable-use and governance framework. A limited proof of concept will validate answer quality, permission handling, logging, content retrieval, and administrative controls.

During months four and five, the project will configure the production environment and prepare the initial knowledge sources. This work will include identity integration, role-based access, content indexing, data-quality remediation, prompt and response controls, monitoring, usage analytics, and support processes. A representative pilot group of approximately 300 employees from corporate, operational, technical, and customer-facing functions will participate in structured testing.

During months six and seven, the pilot will be expanded to approximately 1,000 employees. The project team will evaluate usage, answer accuracy, employee feedback, security events, support volume, and business outcomes. The team will refine the assistant’s configuration, improve source content, resolve access issues, and update training and governance materials based on pilot findings.

During months eight and nine, the assistant will be deployed progressively to the remaining workforce. Rollout will be supported by targeted communications, manager briefings, training sessions, self-service guidance, office hours, and a formal support model. The final month will include a post-implementation review, measurement against success criteria, prioritization of the next wave of integrations and use cases, and transition to steady-state operations.

The phased approach is intended to manage risk, demonstrate value early, and ensure that expansion is based on evidence rather than simple availability of the technology.

## Resource Requirements

The program will require executive sponsorship, dedicated delivery capacity, subject-matter expertise, and ongoing operational ownership. A steering committee comprising representatives from technology, information security, privacy, legal, records management, human resources, communications, and major business units will provide direction and approve significant risk and scope decisions.

The core delivery team should include a program manager, product owner, enterprise architect, AI or platform engineer, data and integration engineers, security and privacy specialists, a data-governance lead, user-experience and accessibility support, change-management and communications leads, training support, business analysts, and representatives from priority business units. During implementation, the organization should plan for approximately 12 to 18 dedicated full-time equivalent resources, supplemented by part-time subject-matter experts and content owners across the business.

Business units will be responsible for identifying and validating priority use cases, assigning owners to authoritative content, reviewing responses in their areas of expertise, and ensuring that outdated or conflicting information is corrected. The technology organization will be responsible for platform administration, integrations, identity and access management, monitoring, service reliability, and technical support. The governance function will oversee policy, risk, compliance, and ongoing use-case approval.

First-year financial requirements are expected to include platform licensing, implementation services, security and architecture work, integration and data preparation, employee training, communications, accessibility, support, and contingency funding. A planning estimate of approximately $1.5 million to $2.5 million should be reserved for the first year, with the final amount determined through platform selection, usage-volume assumptions, integration requirements, and the proportion of implementation work performed internally. Ongoing annual operating costs will include licensing, support, content management, monitoring, training, and continuous improvement.

The deployment will use existing enterprise capabilities wherever practical, including corporate identity services, collaboration tools, security monitoring, service-management processes, and learning platforms. This will reduce duplication and support long-term sustainability.

## Governance, Risk, and Adoption

Trust and responsible use are central to the proposed deployment. The assistant will be configured to respect employee permissions, minimize retention of sensitive prompts and responses, provide appropriate transparency about the sources and limitations of its answers, and maintain audit records sufficient for security and operational review. Data will not be used for model training outside the organization’s approved contractual and technical controls.

Employees will receive clear guidance that AI-generated content may contain errors, omissions, or outdated information. Training will emphasize verification, protection of confidential information, appropriate attribution, accessibility, bias awareness, and the continued need for human accountability. High-impact outputs will require review by an appropriately qualified employee before they are used or distributed.

A formal feedback and incident-management process will allow employees to report inaccurate answers, inappropriate content, security concerns, access problems, and missing information. Usage and performance data will be reviewed regularly by the governance committee, and the organization will retain the ability to suspend individual features, data sources, or use cases when risks exceed approved thresholds.

Adoption will be supported through role-specific examples rather than generic technology demonstrations. Employees will be shown how the assistant can help with tasks relevant to their daily work, while managers will receive guidance on appropriate expectations, productivity measurement, and responsible oversight.

## Success Criteria

The deployment will be considered successful when it demonstrates measurable value, secure operation, and sustainable adoption. Within six months of full rollout, the program should achieve the following targets:

- At least 70 percent of employees have activated the assistant, with at least 50 percent using it monthly.
- At least 60 percent of active users report that the assistant saves meaningful time on information search, drafting, summarization, or related tasks.
- Average time spent locating commonly requested internal information is reduced by at least 25 percent from the baseline established during discovery.
- At least 80 percent of sampled responses to approved knowledge questions are rated accurate and useful by subject-matter reviewers.
- At least 75 percent of pilot and post-launch users rate the assistant as easy to use and appropriately integrated into their workflows.
- No material privacy or security incidents result from the deployment, and all high-severity issues are investigated and resolved within established service levels.
- All production data sources have named owners, documented access rules, and a defined review and refresh process.
- Priority business units have each implemented or approved at least one validated use case beyond general question answering.
- Support volume, system availability, response quality, and usage trends are monitored through an agreed operational dashboard.
- A funded and governed roadmap is approved for the next phase of integrations, workflow automation, and higher-value use cases.

Success will be assessed through a combination of platform analytics, employee surveys, structured quality reviews, help-desk data, security monitoring, time-and-motion studies, and business-unit outcome reporting. The program should proceed to broader automation only when the organization has demonstrated that the assistant is secure, reliable, useful, and trusted.

## Conclusion

Deploying an internal AI assistant across the organization will provide employees with a practical, governed way to access knowledge and complete routine work more efficiently. A phased implementation will allow the organization to realize early benefits while establishing the security, privacy, content, and operating foundations required for responsible scale.

With executive sponsorship, dedicated delivery resources, active participation from business units, and clear measures of success, the organization can introduce AI as a secure enterprise capability rather than a collection of disconnected individual tools. The proposed program will improve productivity, strengthen knowledge access, and create a durable platform for future innovation while preserving human judgment and organizational accountability.

## Background

The organization’s 5,000 employees rely on a wide range of systems, policies, documents, and business processes to perform their work. Information is often distributed across intranet pages, shared drives, knowledge bases, email, collaboration platforms, ticketing systems, and departmental applications. As a result, employees spend significant time locating information, interpreting procedures, drafting routine content, and seeking assistance from subject-matter experts.

The assistant would support employees with activities such as policy and procedure questions, document discovery, meeting and communication drafts, onboarding guidance, service-desk support, data summarization, and workflow navigation. It would operate within the organization’s existing security, identity, privacy, and compliance frameworks, with access determined by each employee’s existing permissions.

This proposal recommends a phased deployment that begins with a controlled pilot, validates value and safeguards, and expands the assistant across the organization based on measurable results. The initiative will combine a centrally governed AI platform with carefully selected integrations, approved use cases, employee training, and continuous monitoring.

## Objectives

The primary objective is to improve employee productivity and access to organizational knowledge while introducing AI in a secure, responsible, and sustainable manner.

The project will pursue the following outcomes:

- Provide employees with a reliable, intuitive assistant for searching approved internal knowledge and completing routine work.
- Reduce the time employees spend locating information, interpreting policies, and producing repetitive documents or communications.
- Improve consistency in the use of organizational policies, procedures, templates, and approved guidance.
- Reduce avoidable demand on service desks and subject-matter experts by resolving routine questions through self-service.
- Establish enterprise standards for AI security, privacy, governance, acceptable use, evaluation, and support.
- Create a scalable foundation for future AI-enabled workflows and departmental applications.
- Ensure that AI outputs are transparent, appropriately qualified, and subject to human review where decisions or risks warrant it.

The program will not position the assistant as a replacement for professional judgment, management responsibility, or formal decision-making. It will be designed to augment employees and direct them to authoritative sources when a question requires escalation or human review.

## Proposed Solution

The organization will deploy a centrally managed internal AI assistant accessible through the company intranet and approved collaboration platforms. Employees will authenticate through the organization’s identity provider and receive responses based on information they are already authorized to access. The assistant will use retrieval-augmented generation to locate relevant content from approved repositories before producing a response, with citations or links to source materials whenever practical.

The initial solution will support general question answering, enterprise knowledge search, document summarization, drafting assistance, onboarding support, and selected service-desk use cases. It will integrate with priority systems such as the intranet, document-management platforms, knowledge bases, human resources content, information technology service management tools, and collaboration systems. Additional integrations will be added only after their data quality, access controls, and business value have been assessed.

The platform will include safeguards against unauthorized data access, prompt injection, inappropriate content generation, accidental disclosure of sensitive information, and overreliance on unsupported answers. High-risk use cases—including employment decisions, legal determinations, financial approvals, safety-critical decisions, and access-control changes—will be excluded from the initial deployment unless separately reviewed and approved through the organization’s governance process.

## Scope

The initial scope includes the design, procurement or configuration, testing, deployment, and support of an enterprise internal AI assistant for all employees. The project will establish the technical platform, connect approved information sources, define governance standards, train users, and measure adoption and business impact.

The first release will focus on a limited set of high-volume, low-to-moderate-risk use cases. These are expected to include:

- Searching and answering questions about internal policies, procedures, benefits, and workplace guidance.
- Finding authoritative documents, templates, forms, and departmental resources.
- Summarizing approved internal documents and meeting materials.
- Drafting routine communications, reports, agendas, and status updates.
- Supporting employee onboarding and navigation of common processes.
- Answering frequently asked information technology and service-desk questions.
- Directing employees to the appropriate team, form, or workflow when the assistant cannot resolve a request.

The project also includes data-source preparation, identity and access integration, security testing, privacy review, records-management review, user education, operational support, and performance reporting.

The initial scope excludes autonomous execution of sensitive transactions, unrestricted access to enterprise data, replacement of existing systems of record, automated employment or financial decisions, and use of unapproved public AI tools with confidential organizational information. Department-specific assistants and advanced workflow automation may be considered in later phases after the core platform has demonstrated acceptable performance and governance maturity.

## Governance, Security, and Responsible Use

A cross-functional AI governance group will oversee the program. Its membership will include representatives from information technology, information security, privacy, legal, records management, human resources, enterprise architecture, risk management, communications, and key business units. The group will approve use cases, classify data, review risks, establish operating policies, and determine when a use case requires additional controls or human approval.

The assistant will use enterprise authentication, role-based access controls, encryption in transit and at rest, audit logging, and centralized monitoring. Source repositories will retain ownership of permissions, and the assistant will not be permitted to expose content beyond an employee’s existing authorization. Administrative access will be limited and reviewed regularly.

Organizational data will not be used to train external foundation models unless explicitly approved through a documented risk and procurement process. Contractual protections will require appropriate data handling, confidentiality, retention, incident notification, and service-level commitments from any technology provider. The project will also establish rules for data retention, conversation history, employee privacy, acceptable use, disclosure of AI assistance, and reporting of incorrect or harmful outputs.

Responses will be evaluated for accuracy, relevance, source traceability, bias, security, and appropriate handling of uncertainty. Where the assistant lacks sufficient evidence, it should state that limitation and direct the employee to an authoritative source or human support channel rather than present an unsupported answer as fact.

## Implementation Timeline

The deployment is expected to take approximately twelve months from initiation through organization-wide release, followed by an ongoing optimization period.

During months one and two, the project team will confirm business requirements, establish governance, select or validate the technology platform, define security and privacy controls, identify priority use cases, and inventory potential information sources. The team will also establish baseline measures for employee effort, service-desk demand, knowledge-search behavior, and user satisfaction.

During months three and four, the organization will prepare the initial content sources and configure the assistant. This phase will include identity integration, access-control validation, document indexing, source-quality assessment, prompt and response standards, monitoring, analytics, and initial user-interface development. A representative test set will be created to evaluate performance across departments and common employee questions.

During months five and six, the assistant will undergo technical, security, privacy, legal, accessibility, and user-acceptance testing. A controlled pilot of approximately 200 to 300 employees will then be conducted across several functions, locations, and levels of technical familiarity. Pilot participants will receive training and will be asked to provide structured feedback on accuracy, usefulness, usability, and trust.

During months seven and eight, the project team will analyze pilot results, correct content and configuration issues, refine governance controls, improve the user experience, and finalize operating procedures. The organization will prepare communications, training materials, support processes, executive guidance, and departmental adoption plans.

During months nine through eleven, the assistant will be rolled out in successive waves to the broader workforce. Each wave will be monitored for performance, adoption, support demand, and emerging risks before the next wave proceeds. Priority departments may receive additional content integration or training support where their use cases demonstrate significant value.

During month twelve, the program will complete the organization-wide launch review, confirm operational ownership, transition the platform to steady-state support, and publish an initial benefits and risk report. After launch, quarterly reviews will assess usage, quality, security events, employee feedback, new use cases, and the continued suitability of the platform and controls.

## Resource Requirements

The program will require executive sponsorship, dedicated project leadership, technical implementation capacity, business participation, and ongoing operational support.

A core implementation team should include a program sponsor, program manager, product owner, enterprise architect, AI or machine-learning engineer, data and integration engineers, information-security specialist, privacy and legal representatives, user-experience designer, content and knowledge-management lead, change-management lead, training and communications specialists, quality-assurance analysts, and support representatives. Business units participating in the pilot should designate subject-matter experts to validate content, define use cases, and review results.

A reasonable initial staffing model is approximately 12 to 18 dedicated full-time-equivalent resources, supplemented by part-time contributors from departments and control functions. After launch, the organization should plan for a standing product and operations team of approximately 6 to 10 full-time-equivalent resources, depending on the number of integrations, usage volume, support model, and pace of new use-case development.

The technology budget will include the AI platform or model services, retrieval and search infrastructure, identity and access integration, data connectors, monitoring and evaluation tools, security testing, implementation services, training, and change management. A preliminary first-year budget range of $2 million to $4 million is appropriate for a 5,000-employee deployment, depending on the selected platform, licensing structure, integration complexity, security requirements, and level of external implementation support. A detailed business case and vendor evaluation should refine this estimate before procurement or contract approval.

The organization will also need to allocate time from information owners and subject-matter experts to review source content, remove obsolete materials, clarify conflicting guidance, and establish ownership for frequently used knowledge. The quality of the assistant will depend substantially on the quality, accessibility, and governance of the underlying information.

## Success Criteria

The project will be considered successful when the assistant is broadly adopted, demonstrably useful, secure, and operationally sustainable. Success will be measured against a baseline established before the pilot and will include both quantitative and qualitative indicators.

Within six months of organization-wide launch, the program should aim for at least 60 percent of employees to have used the assistant and at least 35 percent to use it monthly. At least 75 percent of surveyed users should report that the assistant helps them complete work more efficiently, and at least 80 percent of evaluated responses should be judged accurate, relevant, and appropriately supported by authoritative sources for the approved use cases.

The program should target a 20 percent reduction in time spent answering selected routine internal-information questions, a 15 percent reduction in avoidable service-desk contacts for supported topics, and a measurable improvement in employee satisfaction with knowledge access and onboarding support. For high-volume use cases, the organization should track estimated hours saved, faster completion times, reduction in repeated inquiries, and increased use of approved policies and templates.

Security and governance outcomes are equally important. The assistant must pass required security, privacy, accessibility, and compliance reviews before general release. There should be no material incidents involving unauthorized disclosure of restricted information. All approved use cases must have documented owners, data classifications, risk assessments, monitoring requirements, and escalation procedures. Reported errors and harmful outputs should be logged, investigated, and used to improve the system.

The program should also demonstrate financial and operational sustainability. The organization should be able to explain the platform’s total cost of ownership, maintain acceptable response quality and availability, provide timely user support, and make evidence-based decisions about expanding, modifying, or retiring use cases.

## Conclusion

Deploying an internal AI assistant across the organization represents a practical opportunity to improve employee productivity, strengthen access to institutional knowledge, and establish a disciplined foundation for responsible enterprise AI. A phased approach will allow the organization to demonstrate value while protecting sensitive information, validating user needs, and addressing quality and governance challenges before broad deployment.

With executive sponsorship, strong cross-functional oversight, dedicated implementation resources, and clear success measures, the organization can deliver a secure and useful assistant to its 5,000 employees within approximately twelve months. The resulting capability will provide immediate value through approved knowledge and productivity use cases while creating the technical, organizational, and governance foundation required for future AI-enabled services.

# Proposal: Deployment of an Internal AI Assistant Across the Organization

## Background

The organization’s 5,000 employees rely on a growing collection of documents, systems, policies, knowledge bases, and collaboration tools to complete routine work and make informed decisions. Although this information is valuable, it is often fragmented across intranet pages, shared drives, enterprise applications, ticketing systems, email, and team workspaces. Employees spend significant time searching for information, repeating questions, preparing routine communications, summarizing content, and navigating administrative processes.

Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence make it possible to provide employees with a secure, organization-specific assistant that can help locate and interpret approved internal information, draft and summarize content, answer routine questions, and support common workflows. Deploying such a capability could improve productivity and employee experience while enabling subject-matter experts to focus on higher-value work.

The proposed initiative will establish an internal AI assistant accessible through the organization’s existing collaboration and productivity environment. The assistant will be designed for enterprise use, with strong identity controls, permission-aware information retrieval, auditability, privacy protections, and clear human oversight. It will augment employees rather than replace professional judgment, and it will not make autonomous decisions in sensitive business processes.

## Objectives

The primary objective is to deploy a trusted internal AI assistant that delivers measurable improvements in how employees find information, create content, and complete routine work. The assistant will provide a single, intuitive interface through which employees can ask questions in natural language and receive answers grounded in approved organizational sources.

The initiative will pursue five objectives. First, it will reduce the time employees spend searching for policies, procedures, expertise, and institutional knowledge. Second, it will accelerate routine activities such as drafting emails and documents, summarizing meetings and reports, preparing presentations, and creating first drafts of analysis. Third, it will improve access to consistent and current information by connecting the assistant to authoritative internal sources. Fourth, it will establish a responsible AI operating model covering security, privacy, governance, records management, accessibility, and acceptable use. Finally, it will create a scalable foundation for future AI-enabled workflows without committing the organization prematurely to high-risk or fully autonomous automation.

## Scope

The initial deployment will provide a conversational assistant for all employees, subject to phased access and business-unit readiness. Core capabilities will include question answering over approved internal content, document summarization, drafting and editing, translation where appropriate, meeting and discussion summarization, extraction of key actions and decisions, and assistance with common internal procedures. Responses will include citations or links to source material wherever feasible so that employees can verify information.

The assistant will initially connect to selected enterprise content repositories and collaboration tools, including the intranet, approved policy and procedure libraries, knowledge bases, shared document repositories, and service-management content. Integration with additional systems, such as human resources, finance, customer, legal, or operational platforms, will be evaluated individually and introduced only when data quality, access controls, privacy requirements, and business value have been confirmed.

The deployment will include identity and access management, role-based permissions, logging, usage analytics, content governance, user training, support processes, and an ongoing evaluation program. The solution will respect existing document and system permissions; it will not grant users access to information they could not already access through approved channels.

The first release will exclude autonomous decisions involving employment, compensation, legal determinations, financial approvals, safety-critical operations, or customer commitments. It will also exclude unrestricted ingestion of confidential or regulated data until the relevant controls have been validated. The assistant will be positioned as a support tool, and employees will remain accountable for reviewing outputs and making final decisions.

## Proposed Approach

The organization will use a phased implementation model that balances speed with responsible deployment. The selected technology should support enterprise identity, secure retrieval from internal sources, configurable data retention, administrative controls, model monitoring, audit logs, and the ability to prevent organizational data from being used to train a public model. The final platform decision should be based on security, integration capability, usability, accessibility, total cost of ownership, and the organization’s existing technology ecosystem.

A centralized AI governance group will oversee the program. This group will define acceptable use standards, review high-risk use cases, approve data sources, establish testing requirements, and monitor performance after launch. Security and privacy teams will conduct threat modeling, data protection assessments, access-control reviews, and testing for prompt injection, unauthorized disclosure, hallucination, and misuse. Legal, records management, employee relations, accessibility, and compliance stakeholders will participate as required.

The assistant’s knowledge layer will be built around curated, authoritative content rather than unrestricted access to all organizational data. Each connected source will have an identified business owner, a defined refresh schedule, an access model, and a process for correcting outdated or conflicting information. Responses should favor approved sources, identify uncertainty, and direct users to a human owner or official process when the assistant cannot provide a reliable answer.

Change management will be treated as a core workstream. Employees will receive practical guidance on appropriate use, verification of outputs, protection of sensitive information, and reporting of incorrect or unsafe responses. Managers and subject-matter experts will be engaged early to identify high-value use cases and encourage adoption while preserving accountability.

## Timeline

The proposed implementation timeline is approximately nine months from approval to organization-wide availability.

During months one and two, the program will establish governance, confirm business priorities, select the technology platform, assess data sources, define security and privacy requirements, and document the initial use cases. The team will also establish baseline measures for search time, service-desk demand, employee satisfaction, and other productivity indicators.

During months three and four, the organization will configure the assistant, establish the secure retrieval and identity architecture, connect a limited set of high-quality content sources, and complete initial user-experience design. A controlled technical pilot will test permissions, answer quality, citations, reliability, accessibility, and operational monitoring.

During months five and six, the assistant will be piloted with approximately 300 to 500 employees from representative business areas. The pilot will focus on common use cases such as policy questions, document summarization, drafting, and internal support. Feedback, usage data, security findings, and support trends will be used to improve the solution before expansion.

During months seven and eight, the program will expand access to approximately 1,500 employees across additional functions. Training, communications, support, content remediation, and integration work will be scaled during this period. A formal readiness review will determine whether the assistant meets the required standards for broader deployment.

In month nine, the assistant will become available to the remaining employee population, subject to business-unit readiness and any restrictions identified through the pilot. The launch will be followed by a ninety-day stabilization period focused on performance monitoring, content quality, user support, and prioritization of the next set of integrations and use cases.

## Resource Requirements

The program will require an executive sponsor with authority to resolve cross-functional issues, a full-time product owner, and a program manager responsible for delivery, communications, dependencies, and reporting. A core implementation team should include an enterprise architect, AI or machine-learning engineers, application and integration engineers, data and knowledge-management specialists, security and privacy representatives, a user-experience and accessibility lead, legal and compliance support, change-management and training specialists, and service-desk representatives.

For the initial nine-month deployment, the organization should plan for approximately 12 to 18 dedicated full-time-equivalent staff, supplemented by part-time participation from business-unit subject-matter experts, data owners, legal advisors, records managers, and technology platform teams. After launch, a smaller permanent operating team will be required to manage the product roadmap, content sources, model and prompt configuration, security reviews, analytics, user support, and continuous improvement.

The program budget will include platform or model licensing, secure cloud or hosting capacity, integration development, monitoring and evaluation tools, implementation services where needed, training and communications, accessibility testing, and ongoing support. A contingency should be reserved for content cleanup and access-control remediation, since the quality and structure of existing knowledge repositories will directly affect the assistant’s usefulness and risk profile.

## Success Criteria

The deployment will be considered successful when it demonstrates measurable value without compromising security, privacy, or employee trust. Within six months of broad availability, the organization should target meaningful adoption, with at least 60 percent of employees accessing the assistant and at least 40 percent using it monthly. At least 75 percent of active users should report that the assistant helps them complete work more efficiently, and pilot participants should demonstrate a measurable reduction in time spent locating information or preparing routine content.

The assistant should achieve a high rate of useful, source-supported responses for approved use cases, with answer quality assessed through automated monitoring and regular human evaluation. Critical or high-severity security and privacy incidents must remain at zero, and all identified access-control defects must be remediated before broader rollout. The organization should also track the rate of unsupported or inaccurate answers, successful escalation to human support, content freshness, system availability, response time, and accessibility conformance.

Business units should identify specific productivity or service improvements, such as reduced internal support tickets, faster onboarding, shorter time spent preparing recurring reports, or improved access to policies and procedures. Employee surveys should show increasing confidence in the assistant’s usefulness, transparency, and safeguards. The program should maintain a documented register of use cases, risks, incidents, and benefits so that leadership can evaluate return on investment and determine whether additional automation is justified.

## Conclusion

Deploying an internal AI assistant across a 5,000-employee organization presents a significant opportunity to improve access to knowledge, reduce routine administrative effort, and establish a practical foundation for responsible enterprise AI. The recommended approach combines a focused initial release with strong governance, permission-aware integrations, measurable outcomes, and phased expansion. By treating the assistant as an ongoing product rather than a one-time technology implementation, the organization can deliver near-term value while building the controls, skills, and trust required for broader AI adoption.

# Proposal: Enterprise Deployment of an Internal AI Assistant

## Background

The organization’s 5,000 employees rely on a growing set of systems, documents, policies, and operational processes to complete their work. Important information is often distributed across intranet pages, knowledge bases, shared drives, collaboration platforms, ticketing systems, and business applications. As a result, employees spend significant time searching for information, repeating routine tasks, drafting content, and seeking assistance from subject-matter experts.

Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence make it possible to provide employees with a secure, conversational interface to approved organizational knowledge and productivity tools. An internal AI assistant could help employees find accurate information, summarize documents, draft and improve communications, generate first drafts of reports and procedures, support analysis, and guide users through established business processes. Deployed responsibly, the assistant would augment employees rather than replace human decision-making, while improving speed, consistency, and access to expertise.

This proposal recommends the phased deployment of an enterprise AI assistant for all 5,000 employees. The solution would be designed around the organization’s existing identity, security, collaboration, and data-management environments. It would provide role-appropriate access to approved information, maintain auditability, and include clear safeguards against unauthorized disclosure, inaccurate responses, and inappropriate use.

## Objectives

The primary objective is to give employees a trusted, easy-to-use AI assistant that improves productivity while meeting the organization’s standards for security, privacy, compliance, and responsible technology use.

The initiative will pursue five specific outcomes. First, it will reduce the time employees spend locating and interpreting internal information by providing conversational access to approved policies, procedures, knowledge articles, and business content. Second, it will accelerate common knowledge-work activities such as drafting, summarization, translation, meeting preparation, research, and content transformation. Third, it will improve consistency by directing employees to current, approved sources and standard processes. Fourth, it will establish a scalable governance and operating model for future AI use cases. Finally, it will build employee confidence and adoption through training, transparent communication, and clear guidance on appropriate use.

The assistant will be positioned as a productivity and knowledge-access service. It will not independently make high-impact employment, financial, legal, medical, safety, or customer decisions. Where a response could materially affect a person, transaction, regulatory obligation, or organizational commitment, the assistant will provide support for human review rather than act autonomously.

## Proposed Solution and Scope

The initial solution will be a centrally managed AI assistant accessible through the organization’s approved collaboration and productivity environment, with optional web and mobile access where appropriate. Employees will authenticate through the existing enterprise identity provider, and access to information will be governed by their existing permissions. The assistant will use an approved large language model through an enterprise-controlled service, with a retrieval layer that connects it to selected internal sources.

The first release will support general-purpose capabilities, including answering questions about approved internal policies and procedures, summarizing documents, drafting emails and reports, rewriting content for different audiences, extracting action items, preparing meeting briefs, generating ideas, and helping users navigate internal services. Responses that rely on internal content will include citations or links to source material wherever technically feasible. The assistant will indicate uncertainty and encourage verification when information is incomplete, ambiguous, or potentially consequential.

The scope will include the selection and configuration of the AI platform; integration with enterprise identity and access management; connection to an initial set of high-value and well-governed information sources; security, privacy, and compliance controls; user experience design; pilot deployment; employee enablement; service management; and post-launch measurement.

The initial knowledge sources will be limited to content that is current, owned, appropriately classified, and suitable for broad or role-based access. Likely sources include corporate policies, human resources guidance, information technology support content, procurement procedures, finance guidance, workplace services information, and selected operational knowledge bases. Data owners will approve each source before it is connected. Content that is sensitive, poorly governed, duplicative, obsolete, or subject to unresolved access issues will be excluded until those issues are addressed.

The first phase will not include unrestricted access to all organizational data, autonomous changes to business systems, automated external communications, or unsupervised decisions involving employees, customers, finances, legal matters, safety, or regulatory compliance. Integrations that allow the assistant to create tickets, update records, or initiate workflows may be considered in a later phase after the organization has validated the assistant’s accuracy, authorization model, and audit controls.

## Governance, Security, and Responsible Use

The deployment will be governed by a cross-functional steering group consisting of representatives from executive leadership, information technology, information security, privacy, legal, compliance, human resources, communications, enterprise data, and key business units. This group will approve the initial use cases, risk thresholds, data sources, user policies, and expansion decisions.

The platform will enforce single sign-on, role-based access, encryption in transit and at rest, administrative separation of duties, and detailed logging of system activity. Prompts and responses will be handled according to the organization’s data-classification requirements. Organizational data will not be used to train a public model unless explicitly approved through the organization’s governance process. Controls will be implemented to detect or restrict sensitive personal information, confidential business data, credentials, regulated content, and attempts to bypass security or access restrictions.

The assistant will include visible guidance that responses may contain errors and must be reviewed before being used in consequential work. Users will receive clear instructions about prohibited content, confidential information, intellectual property, records retention, and appropriate human oversight. A feedback and incident-reporting process will allow employees to flag inaccurate answers, unsafe behavior, inappropriate content, access concerns, or missing sources. Reported issues will be triaged through defined service-management procedures, with priority given to privacy, security, and material business-impact events.

## Implementation Timeline

The proposed implementation will occur over approximately nine months, followed by continuous improvement and expansion.

During the first six weeks, the organization will complete discovery, business-case validation, risk assessment, platform selection or confirmation, and solution architecture. This phase will identify priority use cases, establish baseline productivity measures, inventory candidate knowledge sources, assess data quality and permissions, define the responsible-use policy, and confirm the technical and operating model. It will conclude with an approved implementation plan and a decision to proceed into pilot development.

From weeks seven through fourteen, the project team will configure the assistant, establish identity and security integrations, prepare the initial knowledge sources, implement retrieval and citation capabilities, create monitoring dashboards, and develop training materials. A representative group of approximately 250 to 300 employees from different functions and levels will participate in a controlled pilot. Pilot users will test both general productivity capabilities and selected internal knowledge scenarios.

From weeks fifteen through twenty-two, the organization will evaluate the pilot, correct content and access issues, refine prompts and user guidance, validate performance and security controls, and prepare the service for broader adoption. A second release will extend access to approximately 1,000 to 1,500 employees across additional departments. Adoption, response quality, support demand, and risk indicators will be monitored closely during this period.

From weeks twenty-three through thirty-six, the assistant will be rolled out to the remaining employees in successive waves. Each wave will include communications, short role-appropriate training, access to help resources, and a review of early usage and support data. At the end of this period, the steering group will conduct a formal post-launch review and approve the next set of data sources, integrations, and higher-value use cases.

The timeline assumes timely procurement, access to required systems, availability of business and technical subject-matter experts, and no significant remediation delays involving data quality or permissions. The rollout may be adjusted if testing identifies material security, privacy, reliability, or accuracy concerns.

## Resource Requirements

The initiative will require a dedicated product owner with authority to make day-to-day decisions, supported by a program manager responsible for planning, dependencies, risk management, reporting, and coordination across functions. A platform and solution architecture team will configure the AI service, identity integration, retrieval layer, monitoring, and administration model. This team should include enterprise architects, AI or machine-learning engineers, application and integration engineers, data engineers, and platform or cloud specialists.

Security and trust functions will require dedicated participation from information security, privacy, legal, compliance, records management, and, where applicable, labor or employee-relations specialists. Their responsibilities will include risk assessment, policy development, data-source approval, security testing, privacy review, incident response design, and ongoing control monitoring.

Each participating business function will appoint a data owner or subject-matter expert to validate source content, identify priority use cases, test responses, and resolve conflicting or outdated information. A change and adoption team will develop communications, training, manager toolkits, user guidance, champion networks, and feedback processes. Service management and support teams will establish a support model, knowledge articles, escalation procedures, usage monitoring, and service-level expectations.

A core implementation team of approximately 12 to 18 full-time equivalent staff, supplemented by part-time business and control-function contributors, is expected during design and rollout. After deployment, the service should transition to a smaller permanent operating team responsible for product management, platform administration, content and data governance, security oversight, analytics, user support, and continuous improvement. The exact staffing level will depend on the number of connected systems, the degree of customization, and the volume of workflow integrations approved for later phases.

The budget will need to cover enterprise AI platform licensing or consumption, cloud or hosting costs, implementation and integration work, security and privacy assessments, data preparation, user research, training and communications, support operations, monitoring, and contingency for remediation. The organization should also reserve funding for ongoing model evaluation, content governance, accessibility improvements, and future integrations rather than treating the initial launch as a one-time technology purchase.

## Success Criteria

The deployment will be considered successful when the assistant is broadly available, trusted by employees, demonstrably useful, and operating within approved security and governance controls.

Within six months of organization-wide availability, the target is for at least 60 percent of employees to have tried the assistant, with at least 35 percent using it monthly and at least 20 percent using it weekly. Adoption will be evaluated by department and role to identify areas where additional training, better content, or different use cases are needed.

For the initial knowledge scenarios, the assistant should provide a useful answer or source link in at least 85 percent of tested interactions, with factual accuracy meeting an agreed threshold established through representative evaluation sets. Responses involving internal information should cite authoritative sources whenever available, and the rate of materially misleading responses should decline over successive releases. No critical security or privacy incident should be attributable to the platform’s approved configuration, and all identified high-severity issues should have documented remediation or mitigation.

Productivity benefits will be measured against pre-launch baselines. The organization should target a 20 percent reduction in time spent searching for selected internal information, a 15 percent reduction in time required for targeted drafting and summarization activities, and measurable reductions in avoidable support requests for routine policy and process questions. These targets will be validated through usage analytics, employee surveys, time studies, and selected business-process metrics rather than relying solely on self-reported enthusiasm.

Employee experience will also be a key measure. At least 75 percent of active users should report that the assistant helps them complete work more efficiently, and at least 70 percent should indicate that they understand when human review is required. Business units participating in the rollout should have named content owners, current source material, and documented procedures for reporting and resolving inaccurate or unsafe responses.

At the end of the first year, the steering group will review adoption, productivity impact, user satisfaction, security events, support demand, content quality, and financial performance. Based on that review, the organization may expand the assistant’s connected knowledge sources, add carefully governed workflow actions, or adjust the service if expected benefits are not being achieved.

## Recommendation

The organization should proceed with a phased, governed deployment of an internal AI assistant beginning with high-value, low-risk knowledge and productivity use cases. This approach will deliver near-term benefits to employees while creating the security, data, operating, and governance foundations required for more advanced applications. A staged rollout will also allow the organization to measure value, address risks early, improve content quality, and build trust before extending the assistant into more sensitive or action-oriented business processes.

# Proposal: Enterprise Deployment of an Internal AI Assistant

## Background

The organization’s 5,000 employees work across multiple functions, systems, and locations, creating significant demand for fast access to reliable information and routine productivity support. Employees frequently spend time searching for policies, locating documents, summarizing information, drafting communications, preparing reports, and navigating internal processes. These activities are necessary but often repetitive, fragmented across applications, and dependent on individual knowledge of where information resides.

The rapid development of generative AI presents an opportunity to improve employee productivity while strengthening access to institutional knowledge. An internal AI assistant could provide a secure, conversational interface for finding approved company information, summarizing documents, drafting content, answering process questions, and supporting selected business workflows. Deployed responsibly, it would help employees spend less time on administrative work and more time on analysis, customer service, innovation, and decision-making.

The proposed solution will be designed as an enterprise service rather than an uncontrolled collection of individual AI tools. It will operate within the organization’s existing identity, security, compliance, and data-governance frameworks. The assistant will respect each employee’s existing permissions, provide citations or links to source material wherever possible, and make clear when a response requires human review.

## Objectives

The primary objective is to deploy a secure, reliable, and widely adopted AI assistant that improves employee productivity without compromising confidential information, regulatory obligations, or organizational trust.

The assistant will initially focus on five outcomes. First, it will provide permission-aware access to approved internal knowledge, including policies, procedures, standards, training materials, product information, and frequently asked questions. Second, it will support common productivity tasks such as drafting, summarizing, rewriting, translation, meeting preparation, and action-item extraction. Third, it will guide employees through internal processes, including requests, approvals, onboarding, and service interactions. Fourth, it will help functions identify opportunities for automation and better knowledge management. Fifth, it will establish the governance, technical controls, and operating model required for responsible expansion into more advanced use cases.

The program will not position the assistant as a replacement for professional judgment. It will not independently make employment, legal, financial, safety, compliance, or customer-impacting decisions. High-risk use cases will require explicit approval, appropriate human oversight, and additional controls.

## Proposed Solution and Scope

The assistant will be available through the organization’s primary collaboration environment and web applications, with the potential to extend to approved mobile or business-system interfaces after the initial deployment. Employees will authenticate through the organization’s existing single sign-on and multifactor authentication services. Access to information will be governed by existing role-based and attribute-based permissions so that the assistant cannot expose documents or data a user could not already access through authorized systems.

The initial release will use a secure enterprise AI platform capable of connecting to approved content repositories and business applications. It will combine large language models with retrieval from trusted internal sources, allowing responses to be grounded in current company information rather than relying solely on the model’s general knowledge. Responses should include source references where appropriate, and users should be able to provide feedback or report inaccurate, inappropriate, or unsafe answers.

The first release will include enterprise search and question answering, document summarization, drafting and editing assistance, meeting and project support, policy and process guidance, and selected integrations with collaboration, knowledge-management, and service-management platforms. Initial business use cases will be prioritized according to employee reach, expected productivity benefit, data readiness, risk level, and ease of measurement. Likely early adopters include Human Resources, Information Technology, Finance, Legal and Compliance, Operations, Sales, and Corporate Services.

The initial scope will include the design and deployment of the assistant; identity and access integration; approved data connectors; security, privacy, and logging controls; user training; communications; support processes; evaluation and monitoring; and a governance framework for future use cases. It will also include a structured pilot involving representative employees from major business units and geographic regions.

The initial scope will exclude unrestricted access to all enterprise data, autonomous execution of high-impact actions, unsupervised external communications, fully automated decision-making, and the ingestion of unvalidated or poorly governed content. Integrations that can create, approve, delete, or materially change records will require separate risk assessment and explicit authorization.

## Delivery Approach and Timeline

The deployment will be completed over approximately nine months from approval, followed by an ongoing optimization period.

During the first eight weeks, the program will establish its foundation. This phase will confirm executive sponsorship, appoint product and technical owners, define governance standards, select the platform and model approach, complete an initial security and privacy assessment, inventory priority data sources, and identify the first group of business use cases. It will also establish baseline measures for time spent on key tasks, employee search behavior, service-desk demand, and current satisfaction with access to information.

In months three and four, the organization will build and test the minimum viable service. This work will include configuring the AI platform, integrating identity services, connecting a limited set of trusted repositories, implementing permission-aware retrieval, establishing audit logging and monitoring, and creating the initial user experience. A representative pilot of approximately 300 to 500 employees will then evaluate response quality, usefulness, latency, accessibility, security, and user trust. Pilot participants will include both technically confident users and employees with limited prior exposure to AI tools.

In months five and six, the program will refine the assistant based on pilot results and expand it to approximately 1,000 to 1,500 employees across priority functions. This phase will focus on improving source content, addressing recurring failure modes, developing approved prompt patterns and use-case guidance, validating support processes, and confirming that training and communications are effective. Business owners will be required to approve the content and workflows relevant to their functions.

In months seven through nine, the assistant will be rolled out to the remaining employee population in staged waves. Each wave will be supported by targeted communications, brief role-based training, manager enablement, office hours, and clear guidance on appropriate and inappropriate use. Adoption and quality data will be reviewed after each wave, with the ability to pause expansion if security, reliability, or user-trust thresholds are not met.

After the initial rollout, the organization will operate the assistant as a managed product. Quarterly reviews will assess usage, business value, model performance, data quality, emerging risks, and the portfolio of proposed enhancements. New integrations and higher-risk capabilities will be introduced only through the established governance and approval process.

## Resource Requirements

The program will require a dedicated cross-functional team supported by part-time subject-matter experts from across the organization. The core delivery team should include an executive sponsor; a product director or program manager; an AI product manager; enterprise and solution architects; data and integration engineers; security and privacy specialists; legal and compliance representatives; user-experience and accessibility professionals; evaluation and quality specialists; change-management and communications leads; training and support personnel; and business analysts.

A core team of approximately 15 to 20 full-time equivalent staff is recommended during design, build, pilot, and rollout. Additional business participation should come from each major function, including data owners, process owners, knowledge managers, and pilot champions. These contributors will be responsible for validating source content, defining acceptable use, testing outputs, and helping employees adopt the service.

The technical environment will require an enterprise AI platform, model access, secure retrieval and indexing capabilities, data connectors, identity integration, content filtering, monitoring, logging, evaluation tooling, and a support portal. The solution should be configured so that organizational data is not used to train public models unless explicitly approved through a separate governance process. Contracts with technology providers should address data ownership, retention, confidentiality, service availability, incident response, model changes, and audit rights.

A planning estimate for the initial program is approximately $1.5 million to $2.5 million, depending on platform selection, integration complexity, data remediation requirements, and the amount of internal engineering capacity available. Ongoing annual operating costs are expected to be approximately $1 million to $2 million, including model usage, platform licensing, infrastructure, support, security monitoring, evaluation, training, and continuous improvement. These figures should be refined during the foundation phase and presented for approval through the organization’s normal investment process.

## Governance, Risk, and Responsible Use

The assistant will be governed by a cross-functional AI steering committee with authority from Technology, Information Security, Privacy, Legal, Compliance, Human Resources, and representative business functions. The committee will approve use-case categories, establish risk tiers, review incidents, and determine when additional controls or human review are required.

The service will enforce least-privilege access, maintain audit logs, protect sensitive information, and apply retention and deletion rules consistent with existing policy. Security testing will include prompt-injection testing, unauthorized data-access testing, harmful-content testing, data-leakage testing, and resilience testing. The assistant will provide user-facing guidance that responses may contain errors and should be verified before being used in consequential situations.

Content quality will be treated as a shared organizational responsibility. Each connected repository will have a designated owner, an approved classification, defined retention rules, and a process for correcting outdated or contradictory information. The assistant will be evaluated not only on whether an answer sounds plausible, but also on whether it is accurate, grounded in approved sources, appropriately cautious, and useful for the intended task.

## Success Criteria

The deployment will be considered successful when the assistant is available to all eligible employees, operates within approved security and privacy controls, and demonstrates measurable value in daily work. Within six months of full rollout, the target is for at least 70 percent of employees to have used the assistant and for at least 50 percent to use it monthly. Adoption will be assessed alongside satisfaction, repeat usage, and usage across functions to ensure the service is not limited to a small group of early adopters.

The assistant should achieve an average user satisfaction score of at least 4 out of 5 for supported use cases and deliver a grounded, acceptable response in at least 85 percent of evaluated test scenarios. Critical privacy or security incidents attributable to the service should remain at zero, with all lower-severity incidents investigated and resolved according to defined service levels.

Business value will be measured through a combination of user research, task-time studies, workflow metrics, and operational indicators. The initial target is a 20 percent reduction in time spent on selected activities such as information retrieval, document summarization, routine drafting, and process navigation. Participating functions should also identify measurable improvements in service response times, employee self-service, onboarding efficiency, or knowledge reuse.

Finally, the program should establish a sustainable operating model. This means that priority data sources have named owners, new use cases are assessed through a consistent governance process, employees understand responsible-use expectations, support teams can resolve issues effectively, and leadership receives regular reporting on adoption, performance, risk, and return on investment.

## Conclusion

Deploying an internal AI assistant across the organization is an opportunity to improve productivity, make institutional knowledge easier to use, and create a controlled foundation for broader AI innovation. A phased, permission-aware, human-centered approach will allow the organization to capture value quickly while protecting confidential information and maintaining accountability. With executive sponsorship, dedicated cross-functional resources, disciplined governance, and measurable success criteria, the organization can deliver a trusted AI capability that supports all 5,000 employees and evolves with business needs.
