To deliver these benefits responsibly, the assistant must be introduced through a structured program that prioritizes information security, privacy, governance, accuracy, user adoption, and measurable business value.

This proposal recommends the phased deployment of an enterprise internal AI assistant for the organization’s approximately 5,000 employees. The program will establish a secure AI platform, connect it to approved internal information sources, launch high-value use cases, and create the operating model required to manage the assistant over time.

## Objectives

The primary objective is to give employees a trusted, easy-to-use assistant that improves access to organizational knowledge and reduces time spent on repetitive knowledge work. The assistant will provide answers grounded in approved internal content, cite the sources used, and clearly distinguish between retrieved organizational information and generated content.

The program will pursue five related objectives. First, it will improve employee productivity by supporting activities such as research, summarization, drafting, translation, meeting preparation, and information retrieval. Second, it will make institutional knowledge more accessible by allowing employees to search across approved repositories using natural language rather than relying on fragmented keywords and folder structures. Third, it will improve consistency by directing employees to current policies, procedures, templates, and approved guidance. Fourth, it will reduce the burden on help desks and subject-matter experts by resolving routine questions and routing more complex requests appropriately. Finally, it will establish a sustainable foundation for future AI-enabled workflows while maintaining appropriate controls over confidential information, personal data, and business-critical decisions.

The assistant will support employees rather than replace professional judgment. It will not be authorized to make high-impact decisions independently, provide unsupervised legal, financial, medical, employment, or regulatory determinations, or take irreversible actions without explicit user confirmation and appropriate controls.

## Scope

The initial deployment will provide a secure conversational assistant accessible through the organization’s existing identity and collaboration environment. Employees will authenticate using corporate single sign-on, and access to information will be governed by their existing roles and permissions. The assistant will be available through a web interface and, where practical, integrated into the organization’s primary collaboration platform.

Initial capabilities will include enterprise search and question answering across approved internal content; summarization of documents, email threads, and meeting transcripts; drafting and editing of routine business communications; creation of first drafts for reports, presentations, project plans, and other common documents; translation and rewriting; preparation of meeting agendas and action items; and guidance on internal policies and procedures. Responses will include links or citations to source materials whenever the assistant relies on indexed organizational content.

The first information sources will be selected based on business value, content quality, permission consistency, and technical readiness. These may include the corporate intranet, policy library, document management platform, approved knowledge bases, human resources guidance, information technology support content, procurement procedures, and selected operational repositories. Additional systems, including ticketing, customer relationship management, project management, and workflow platforms, may be connected during later phases after security and process reviews.

The program includes the establishment of AI governance, privacy and security controls, content and data-readiness activities, user training, technical support, performance monitoring, and an ongoing improvement process. It also includes development of a formal acceptable-use policy, data classification guidance, human-review requirements, incident-response procedures, and a process for approving new integrations and use cases.

The initial scope excludes autonomous execution of high-risk transactions, unrestricted access to all enterprise data, use of personal or confidential information in unapproved external AI services, and replacement of existing systems of record. The assistant will not serve as the authoritative source for policies or business records; it will help employees locate and interpret approved sources, which will remain under the ownership of the relevant business functions.

## Delivery Approach and Timeline

The program will be delivered over approximately twelve months in four phases, followed by an ongoing operating period.

During months one and two, the organization will establish the program foundation. This phase will confirm executive sponsorship, appoint a product owner, define governance and decision rights, document priority use cases, assess the existing data and technology environment, and complete the initial privacy, security, legal, and risk assessments. The team will select the AI platform and model strategy, define the target architecture, establish success baselines, and identify the initial group of content repositories. Approximately 50 to 75 employees from representative business functions will participate in discovery and design activities.

During months three through five, the program will build and validate the minimum viable product. The delivery team will implement single sign-on, role-based access controls, audit logging, data-loss prevention controls, content connectors, retrieval and citation capabilities, feedback mechanisms, and administrative dashboards. Initial content will be cleaned, classified, and indexed. The assistant will be tested against representative questions and documents, including attempts to expose restricted information, generate unsupported answers, or follow malicious instructions embedded in source content. A controlled pilot of approximately 300 employees will then begin, representing corporate functions, operations, managers, technical teams, and other major user groups.

During months six through eight, the program will evaluate the pilot and expand the service. The team will improve retrieval quality, response accuracy, user experience, performance, and support processes based on pilot feedback. High-value integrations, such as IT service guidance, human resources policy lookup, procurement assistance, and meeting or document summarization, will be added where they meet the required controls. Training materials, communications, usage guidance, and manager enablement will be finalized. The user population will expand to approximately 1,000 employees, with particular emphasis on functions that demonstrate measurable productivity opportunities.

During months nine through twelve, the assistant will be deployed broadly to the remaining employee population in controlled waves. Each wave will be supported by communications, role-specific training, office hours, and adoption monitoring. The team will conduct a formal benefits review, remediate outstanding risks, establish service-level expectations, and transition the assistant from a project into a managed enterprise service. At the end of this phase, the organization will have a documented roadmap for additional data sources, workflow actions, specialized assistants, and future model or platform enhancements.

After the initial twelve-month deployment, the assistant will operate as a continuously managed product. Quarterly reviews will assess adoption, business value, content quality, security events, model performance, and emerging risks. New integrations and higher-impact capabilities will be introduced only through the established governance process.

## Resource Requirements

The program will require a dedicated core team supported by part-time representatives from business and control functions. The core delivery team should include a program or product lead, an enterprise architect, two to three AI or machine-learning engineers, two application and integration engineers, one data or knowledge engineer, one security engineer, one privacy and risk specialist, one user-experience or service designer, one test and evaluation lead, one change-management and communications lead, and one training and support lead. During the deployment period, this represents approximately 14 to 18 full-time equivalent roles, with staffing adjusted as the service moves from implementation into steady-state operations.

Business participation will include designated content owners from human resources, information technology, legal, finance, procurement, operations, communications, and other major functions. These representatives will validate source content, approve use cases, define escalation paths, and help measure business outcomes. The legal, privacy, security, records-management, accessibility, and employee-relations functions should each provide a named approver or advisor. Their involvement is expected to average part-time across the program, increasing during design reviews, pilot approval, and the transition to broad deployment.

The technology environment should include an enterprise-grade large language model provider or approved internal model, a retrieval and indexing layer, secure data connectors, identity and access-management integration, monitoring and audit capabilities, content filtering, data-loss prevention, and an administrative console. The selected architecture should support model substitution where practical to reduce vendor dependency and allow the organization to balance performance, cost, residency, and risk requirements over time.

A preliminary first-year budget of approximately $3 million to $5 million is recommended, subject to final platform selection, usage volumes, integration complexity, and the proportion of internal versus vendor-hosted infrastructure. This estimate includes implementation staffing, model and platform consumption, security and monitoring tools, data preparation, integration work, training, communications, user support, accessibility testing, and contingency funding. Ongoing annual operating costs should be planned separately for model usage, platform licensing, content maintenance, engineering support, governance, and user enablement.

## Security, Privacy, and Governance

The assistant will operate within the organization’s existing security and privacy framework and will not create a separate access model that bypasses established controls. It will enforce corporate identity, role-based permissions, data classification requirements, and repository-level access rights. Users will receive only information they are already authorized to access, and all prompts, retrieved content, responses, administrative actions, and material configuration changes will be logged in accordance with records-retention and privacy requirements.

Confidential and personal information will be protected through approved data-handling rules, encryption in transit and at rest, retention controls, vendor contractual safeguards, and data-loss prevention policies. Prompts and organizational content will not be used to train external foundation models unless explicitly approved under the organization’s contractual, legal, and privacy requirements. The program will also test for prompt injection, unauthorized data retrieval, hallucinations, bias, harmful content, insecure tool use, and attempts to manipulate the assistant through malicious documents or instructions.

A cross-functional AI Governance Committee will oversee use-case approval, risk classification, model and vendor decisions, policy development, incident response, and periodic control reviews. Each connected content source will have an accountable owner responsible for accuracy, currency, access permissions, and retirement of obsolete material. Use cases involving regulated data, employment decisions, financial approvals, customer commitments, or external communications will require enhanced review and human approval.

## Success Criteria

The program will be considered successful when the assistant is broadly available, trusted by employees, demonstrably useful, and operating within defined security and governance controls. Within six months of broad deployment, the target is for at least 60 percent of employees to have used the assistant and for at least 40 percent to use it monthly. Adoption will be evaluated by role and function rather than only in aggregate to ensure that access and training are equitable across the organization.

For priority use cases, the organization will target a 20 percent reduction in time spent on information retrieval, summarization, drafting, and routine policy questions, measured through baseline studies, user surveys, task sampling, and operational metrics. At least 70 percent of pilot and early-adopter users should report that the assistant improves their ability to complete routine knowledge work. Support functions using the assistant for internal questions should achieve a measurable reduction in repetitive inquiries or a corresponding improvement in response times.

Quality targets will include at least 90 percent citation coverage for answers based on indexed internal content, at least 85 percent correctness on an approved evaluation set for priority use cases, and a clear user experience for reporting incorrect or unsafe responses. The service should meet agreed availability and performance targets, with typical responses delivered within a reasonable enterprise-service standard and with transparent communication when information is unavailable or confidence is low.

Security and governance success will require no critical data-exposure incidents, completion of required privacy and security assessments before each deployment stage, full auditability of administrative and user activity, and documented ownership for every connected information source. All employees will receive acceptable-use guidance, and users in higher-risk functions will complete role-specific training before receiving access to advanced capabilities.

The program will also establish a positive return-on-investment case for continued funding. By the end of the first year, the organization should be able to quantify productivity gains, avoided support effort, improved knowledge access, and user satisfaction, while documenting the costs and risks associated with operating the service. These findings will guide decisions about additional integrations, workflow automation, specialized assistants, and future expansion.

## Recommendation

Approval is recommended for the twelve-month phased deployment of the internal AI assistant, beginning with program mobilization, governance, and a controlled pilot before organization-wide release. This approach balances the opportunity to improve productivity and knowledge access with the need to protect sensitive information, validate business value, and establish responsible operating practices. With executive sponsorship, dedicated cross-functional resources, and disciplined measurement, the organization can provide a practical AI capability to all 5,000 employees while creating a secure foundation for broader digital transformation.

The deployment will be considered successful when the assistant is available to all intended employees through approved channels, operates within the organization’s security and privacy requirements, and is supported by a sustainable service and governance model. Within six months of enterprise rollout, the program should achieve meaningful regular use across participating business units, with at least 60 percent of enabled employees trying the service and at least 35 percent using it monthly. User satisfaction should reach a minimum average rating of 4 out of 5, and at least 70 percent of surveyed users should report that the assistant saves time or improves their ability to complete routine work.

For priority knowledge-retrieval use cases, the organization should target a measurable reduction in time spent locating information, with a goal of reducing average search and navigation time by at least 25 percent. For selected drafting, summarization, and research activities, users should report productivity improvements of at least 15 percent, subject to validation through representative workflow studies. The program should also demonstrate improved access to authoritative content through source-linked responses and a reduction in repetitive questions directed to designated support teams.

Risk and quality measures will be equally important. The service should maintain a documented process for reporting and correcting inaccurate responses, complete required security and privacy reviews, achieve full training and responsible-use acknowledgement for enabled employees, and record no material privacy or security incidents attributable to inadequate deployment controls. High-risk requests should be appropriately restricted or routed for human review. Business units should be able to demonstrate that employees understand when AI assistance is permitted and when independent professional review is required.

At the end of the first year, the executive sponsor and steering group will review adoption, productivity benefits, user experience, operating costs, incidents, and business-unit feedback. The review will determine whether to expand integrations, introduce workflow automation, revise controls, or redirect investment toward the use cases delivering the greatest organizational value. Through this phased and governed approach, the organization can establish an internal AI capability that improves employee effectiveness while preserving trust, accountability, and control.

# Project Proposal: Enterprise Internal AI Assistant

## Background

The organization’s 5,000 employees rely on a wide range of information sources, business systems, policies, and subject-matter experts to complete routine work. Important knowledge is distributed across intranet pages, collaboration platforms, document repositories, ticketing systems, operating procedures, and individual teams. As a result, employees often spend substantial time searching for information, recreating existing content, waiting for answers from specialist teams, and completing administrative tasks manually.

An internal AI assistant can provide a secure, governed interface for finding organizational knowledge, summarizing information, drafting content, answering policy and process questions, and supporting routine workflows. Used appropriately, it can improve employee productivity and access to expertise while reducing repetitive work for service teams such as Human Resources, Information Technology, Legal, Finance, Procurement, and Operations.

The proposed initiative will deploy a centrally governed AI assistant for all employees, beginning with a controlled pilot and expanding through measured releases. The assistant will use approved enterprise data sources, respect existing access permissions, maintain clear boundaries around high-risk use cases, and provide monitoring and feedback mechanisms throughout its lifecycle.

## Objectives

The primary objective is to establish a trusted, secure, and useful AI capability that helps employees complete work more efficiently without compromising confidentiality, regulatory obligations, or business controls.

The assistant will provide employees with a single conversational entry point for approved internal knowledge. It will answer questions using authoritative company content, cite or link to source material where possible, summarize documents and discussions, draft routine communications and business documents, and help users navigate established processes. It will also support selected workflow integrations, such as creating service requests, locating forms, checking process status, or preparing structured information for human review.

The initiative will pursue five specific outcomes. First, it will reduce the time employees spend locating information and completing repetitive knowledge work. Second, it will improve consistency in the use of policies, procedures, and approved content. Third, it will expand access to specialist knowledge while preserving the role of subject-matter experts. Fourth, it will establish enterprise standards for responsible AI use, including security, privacy, records management, accessibility, and human oversight. Fifth, it will create a scalable foundation for future AI-enabled workflows based on evidence from the initial deployment.

## Scope

The initial solution will be available to all employees through the organization’s standard collaboration and productivity environment, with access controlled through existing identity and authorization systems. Users will authenticate through single sign-on, and the assistant will apply role-based and source-system permissions so that it does not expose information a user could not already access. The experience will be optimized for desktop and mobile use where supported by the selected platform.

The first release will include conversational search across approved internal knowledge sources, question answering with source references, document summarization, meeting and discussion summarization where authorized, drafting and rewriting assistance, translation and accessibility support, and guidance through common corporate processes. Priority knowledge sources will include the intranet, enterprise policy libraries, employee handbooks, IT and HR knowledge bases, approved operating procedures, service catalogs, and selected collaboration repositories.

The project will also develop a limited set of workflow integrations in partnership with business owners. Examples may include initiating an IT support request, locating an HR form, identifying the correct procurement process, preparing a standard case summary, or routing a request to the appropriate service team. Any action that changes a system of record, creates an external commitment, makes an employment decision, provides legal or financial advice, or affects an individual’s rights will require explicit user confirmation and, where appropriate, human approval.

The deployment will not initially include fully autonomous decision-making, unsupervised external communications, automated personnel decisions, unrestricted access to confidential repositories, or the use of unapproved public AI tools with company data. The assistant will not be positioned as a replacement for professional judgment. Responses will include appropriate notices that AI-generated content may require verification, particularly for legal, financial, medical, security, employment, and regulatory matters.

The project scope includes platform selection or configuration, security and privacy assessment, data-source preparation, permission mapping, user experience design, integration development, testing, training, communications, adoption support, monitoring, and post-launch governance. It also includes the creation of an enterprise AI usage policy, content ownership standards, incident management procedures, and a process for evaluating future use cases.

## Delivery Approach and Timeline

The program will be delivered over approximately twelve months in five phases, followed by ongoing operation and continuous improvement.

During Months 1 and 2, the project team will establish the program foundation. This phase will confirm executive sponsorship, appoint business and technology owners, document the target operating model, select or confirm the AI platform, define security and privacy requirements, inventory candidate knowledge sources, and establish baseline measures for productivity, search effectiveness, employee satisfaction, and service-team workload. The team will also define acceptable-use rules, data-handling standards, escalation procedures, and a formal risk register.

During Months 3 and 4, the team will prepare the initial knowledge and technical environment. Priority content will be reviewed for accuracy, ownership, duplication, currency, classification, and accessibility. Connectors will be configured for approved repositories, and identity, access-control, logging, retention, and monitoring capabilities will be tested. The team will build the initial assistant experience, establish response and citation standards, and conduct security testing, privacy reviews, prompt-injection testing, and adversarial evaluation using representative business scenarios.

During Months 5 and 6, the organization will conduct a controlled pilot with approximately 300 to 500 employees representing corporate functions, frontline operations, managers, technical teams, and other major user groups. Pilot users will receive training and clear guidance on appropriate use. The team will measure response quality, source accuracy, task completion time, user satisfaction, adoption, access-control performance, and support demand. Pilot results will be reviewed through formal go/no-go criteria before expansion.

During Months 7 through 9, the assistant will be refined and expanded to approximately 1,500 to 2,000 employees. Additional knowledge domains and a small number of workflow integrations will be introduced only after their content quality, ownership, security, and support models have been approved. The program will launch a broader communications and training campaign, establish an employee feedback community, publish role-specific examples, and equip managers and service teams to support adoption.

During Months 10 through 12, the assistant will be made available across the full 5,000-employee organization, subject to completion of readiness criteria. The final phase will focus on operational stabilization, performance tuning, content stewardship, support processes, accessibility validation, and benefits measurement. At the end of Month 12, the program will produce an operational review covering adoption, productivity benefits, risk events, user feedback, costs, and recommendations for the next release cycle.

After the initial deployment, the assistant will operate as an enduring enterprise service rather than a one-time technology project. New data sources, integrations, and use cases will be prioritized through a governance process based on business value, risk, data readiness, and measurable outcomes.

## Resource Requirements

The program will require a cross-functional team led by an executive sponsor and a dedicated program director. During implementation, the core team should include an AI product manager, enterprise architect, security architect, privacy and compliance lead, data and knowledge-management lead, user experience designer, integration engineers, platform and identity specialists, test and quality leads, change-management and communications professionals, training and adoption leads, and service-management representatives. A core team of approximately 15 to 20 full-time equivalent staff, supplemented by part-time subject-matter experts, is expected to be sufficient for the initial deployment. The precise staffing level will depend on the selected platform and the number of integrations included.

Each participating business function will appoint a content owner and an AI product representative. Content owners will be responsible for the accuracy, currency, classification, and retirement of information made available to the assistant. Subject-matter experts will help define high-value use cases, validate responses, establish escalation paths, and identify content gaps. Department leaders will support adoption, reinforce responsible-use expectations, and ensure that the assistant complements rather than bypasses established controls.

The technical environment will require an enterprise AI platform or managed model service that supports private organizational use, contractual data protections, administrative controls, audit logging, access-aware retrieval, model and prompt configuration, usage analytics, and integration with the organization’s identity and collaboration systems. Infrastructure will also be needed for secure connectors, indexing and retrieval, application monitoring, content management, test environments, service support, and backup or recovery capabilities where applicable. All data flows will be documented and reviewed before production use.

The program will require funding for platform licensing or consumption, implementation services, integration development, security and privacy assessments, user research, training, communications, content remediation, and ongoing operational support. A detailed budget will be finalized during the foundation phase after platform selection and integration sizing. The business case should account not only for software costs but also for the effort required to improve source content, maintain permissions, govern use cases, and support employees after launch.

## Governance, Security, and Responsible Use

The assistant will be governed by an enterprise AI steering committee comprising representatives from Technology, Information Security, Privacy, Legal, Risk, Human Resources, Records Management, Compliance, Operations, and key business functions. The committee will approve the initial scope, review high-impact use cases, monitor performance and incidents, and set standards for future expansion.

Security and privacy controls will include single sign-on, least-privilege access, encryption in transit and at rest, segregation of environments, administrative role separation, audit logging, retention controls, data-loss prevention, and continuous monitoring. The assistant will retrieve information only from approved sources and will preserve source-system permissions wherever technically feasible. Sensitive data categories will be evaluated individually, and content will not be onboarded solely because it is technically accessible.

The program will establish testing for hallucination, inaccurate citations, unauthorized disclosure, prompt injection, data poisoning, harmful or biased responses, unsafe automation, and inappropriate reliance. High-risk outputs will require human review, and users will have a clear mechanism to report incorrect, unsafe, or inappropriate responses. Incidents will be investigated through established security, privacy, and service-management procedures.

The organization will publish a practical acceptable-use policy explaining what employees may enter into the assistant, how outputs should be validated, which decisions may not be delegated, and how concerns should be reported. Training will be mandatory for initial users and incorporated into onboarding and recurring awareness programs.

## Success Criteria

The deployment will be considered successful when it demonstrates measurable value, responsible operation, and sustainable adoption. By the end of the first twelve months, the program will target at least 70 percent awareness among employees, at least 50 percent monthly active usage among the intended user population, and sustained usage across all major business functions rather than concentration in a small group of early adopters.

For priority knowledge and process questions, the assistant should achieve a validated answer usefulness rate of at least 80 percent, with source references available for the large majority of knowledge-based responses. User testing should show a 25 percent or greater reduction in time spent locating information or completing selected routine tasks. Participating service teams should identify measurable reductions in repetitive inquiries, avoidable ticket volume, or time spent preparing standard responses, with targets established separately for each use case.

The program should achieve a user satisfaction score of at least 4 out of 5 among active users and demonstrate that employees can complete core tasks without unacceptable accessibility barriers. Training completion, policy acknowledgment, and support readiness should exceed 90 percent for required groups. All production data sources must have named owners, documented permissions, classification decisions, and review schedules.

From a risk perspective, there should be no material security or privacy incidents attributable to unauthorized assistant access or uncontrolled data disclosure. Critical vulnerabilities identified during testing must be resolved before production expansion, and all high-risk use cases must have documented human-approval controls. The organization should also maintain a complete audit trail of administrative activity, integrations, incidents, model or prompt changes, and governance decisions.

At the end of the first year, the executive steering committee will review the results against these measures and determine the next investment priorities. Continued expansion will be based on demonstrated business value, reliable content, employee trust, manageable operating costs, and the organization’s ability to maintain appropriate human oversight. This approach will allow the organization to capture the benefits of internal AI assistance while establishing the controls and operating discipline required for long-term, responsible use.

# Project Proposal: Enterprise Internal AI Assistant Deployment

## Background

The organization’s 5,000 employees rely on information distributed across intranet pages, document repositories, collaboration platforms, service desks, policy libraries, and business applications. As a result, employees spend significant time searching for answers, recreating existing materials, summarizing information, and completing repetitive administrative tasks. Support functions such as IT, Human Resources, Legal, Finance, and Operations also spend substantial capacity responding to routine questions that could be addressed through well-governed self-service.

Public generative AI tools offer some productivity benefits, but their use for internal work can create unacceptable risks related to confidentiality, privacy, intellectual property, inconsistent answers, and regulatory compliance. A secure internal AI assistant would provide employees with a controlled way to search organizational knowledge, draft and summarize content, and receive assistance with approved workflows while maintaining existing access controls and human accountability.

This proposal recommends a phased deployment of an enterprise AI assistant for all 5,000 employees. The solution will use approved AI models together with permission-aware retrieval of internal information, ensuring that users can access only the content they are already authorized to view. The deployment will establish a foundation for responsible AI adoption while delivering measurable improvements in productivity, knowledge access, and employee experience.

## Objectives

The primary objective is to make reliable organizational knowledge easier to find and use. Employees should be able to ask questions in natural language, receive concise answers supported by links or citations to approved internal sources, and quickly locate the documents, policies, procedures, and expertise they need.

The project will also reduce the time required for common knowledge-work activities, including drafting emails and reports, summarizing meetings and documents, preparing first drafts of presentations, comparing policies, creating service responses, and converting information into standardized formats. The assistant will support—not replace—employee judgment, with users remaining responsible for reviewing and approving material before it is shared or used in business decisions.

A further objective is to create a scalable governance and operating model for future AI capabilities. This will include clear policies for acceptable use, data protection, human oversight, model evaluation, incident management, and ongoing improvement. The program will establish a repeatable method for introducing additional AI-enabled workflows without compromising security, privacy, or regulatory obligations.

## Scope

The initial solution will provide a secure conversational interface accessible through the organization’s approved collaboration environment and web portal. It will support question answering over approved enterprise content, document and meeting summarization, drafting and rewriting, information extraction, translation where appropriate, and guided assistance for common IT, HR, Finance, and operational processes.

The assistant will connect to selected sources such as the intranet, policy repositories, knowledge bases, document management platforms, service-management content, and other approved systems. Integration will be introduced incrementally, beginning with high-value, well-governed content. Each source will be assessed for ownership, accuracy, classification, access permissions, retention requirements, and readiness for AI use.

The technical design will use enterprise identity and access management, single sign-on, role-based permissions, encryption, audit logging, data-loss prevention controls, and defined retention settings. Responses will be grounded in approved internal sources wherever possible and will identify the sources used. Company data will not be used to train external models unless explicitly approved through the organization’s governance process and contractual protections are in place.

The project will include the development of an AI usage policy, employee training, administrator procedures, content ownership standards, evaluation benchmarks, and a support model. It will also establish a process for reporting inaccurate responses, inappropriate content, security concerns, and other incidents.

The initial scope will not include autonomous decisions or actions in high-impact areas such as hiring, termination, compensation, legal determinations, financial approvals, medical decisions, or regulatory submissions. The assistant will not replace systems of record, bypass existing approval processes, or execute transactions without explicit authorization and appropriate human review. These capabilities may be considered in later phases only after separate risk assessment and approval.

## Implementation Timeline

The deployment will be completed through a 12-month phased program.

During Months 1 and 2, the project team will conduct discovery and establish the foundation for delivery. This phase will confirm priority use cases, identify target user groups, document current-state productivity and support baselines, assess available content sources, select the implementation approach, and complete initial security, privacy, legal, procurement, and architecture reviews. An executive steering committee and an AI governance working group will be established during this period.

During Months 3 and 4, the team will configure the platform and build the first controlled version of the assistant. This work will include identity integration, permission-aware content retrieval, initial data connectors, user experience design, response citation, logging, monitoring, evaluation tools, and administrator controls. Security testing, privacy assessment, accessibility review, and content-quality checks will occur before any broad employee access is granted.

During Months 5 and 6, the assistant will be piloted with approximately 300 to 500 employees representing different functions, roles, technical abilities, and levels of information sensitivity. The pilot will focus on approved use cases such as enterprise knowledge search, IT and HR self-service, document summarization, and drafting. Feedback, usage data, response-quality evaluations, and support issues will be used to refine the solution and finalize the enterprise operating model.

During Months 7 and 8, the service will expand to approximately 1,500 employees. The project team will improve source content, add approved integrations, strengthen training and communications, and validate that performance, security, support, and governance processes work at greater scale. Departmental champions will help identify local use cases and reinforce responsible adoption.

At the end of Month 12, the program will complete a formal benefits review and present recommendations for the next phase, including additional workflows, deeper system integrations, and any approved transactional capabilities.

## Resource Requirements

The program will require an executive sponsor with authority to resolve cross-functional issues and maintain organizational alignment. A steering committee should include representatives from Technology, Information Security, Privacy, Legal, Human Resources, Operations, Communications, and key business units. An AI governance group will oversee acceptable use, risk classification, content eligibility, evaluation standards, and incident response.

A core implementation team of approximately 12 to 16 full-time-equivalent resources will be required during the first year. This team should include a product owner, program manager, enterprise or AI architect, platform and integration engineers, data engineers, identity and security specialists, a privacy or data-governance lead, an evaluation and quality lead, a user-experience or conversation designer, a change-management and training lead, and a service-support lead. Legal, procurement, accessibility, records-management, and compliance specialists should participate on a part-time basis as needed.

Content owners will be responsible for the accuracy, classification, currency, and retirement of information made available to the assistant. The technical environment will require an enterprise-grade AI platform or approved model provider, secure hosting, identity and access integration, document and knowledge connectors, monitoring, audit capability, evaluation tooling, and sufficient capacity for approximately 5,000 users. The organization should also budget for licensing, implementation services where needed, employee training, communications, content remediation, ongoing platform operations, and continuous model and security evaluation.

Following deployment, the assistant should transition to a standing operating model consisting of a product owner, platform and data support, security and governance oversight, content owners, and a user-support function. This team will manage releases, evaluate new use cases, monitor performance, and ensure that the assistant remains aligned with organizational policies and business needs.

## Success Criteria

# Project Proposal: Enterprise Internal AI Assistant

## Background

The organization’s 5,000 employees rely on a growing collection of documents, policies, applications, knowledge bases, collaboration channels, and service systems to perform their work. Although this information is valuable, it is often difficult to locate, interpret, and apply consistently. Employees spend significant time searching across disconnected systems, repeating questions, drafting routine content, and routing requests to specialist teams.

Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence create an opportunity to improve this experience through a secure internal assistant. The assistant would provide employees with a single, conversational way to search approved organizational knowledge, summarize information, draft content, answer routine questions, and support selected business workflows. It would operate within existing identity, access, security, privacy, and records-management controls rather than creating an uncontrolled alternative to them.

The proposed initiative will establish a governed enterprise AI capability that improves productivity while protecting confidential information and maintaining human accountability. The project will begin with a controlled pilot, use measured evidence to refine the service, and then expand across the organization in stages.

## Objectives

The primary objective is to give employees fast, reliable, and appropriately permissioned access to the information and assistance they need to do their work. The assistant will help users find answers across approved sources, summarize policies and documents, draft routine communications and reports, prepare for meetings, and navigate common IT, HR, finance, and operational processes.

The project will also reduce avoidable demand on service teams by providing accurate answers to frequently asked questions and routing more complex requests to the appropriate human experts. It will create a consistent foundation for future AI-enabled workflows while establishing standards for responsible use, data protection, model governance, and ongoing performance evaluation.

By the end of the first year, the organization should have an assistant available to all employees for approved use cases, a repeatable process for adding new data sources and capabilities, a trained network of business champions, and a governance model capable of managing future AI applications.

The assistant will not make final decisions on behalf of managers or professional functions, independently approve transactions, evaluate employee performance, provide unsupervised legal or medical advice, or access information that a user is not already authorized to view. Any workflow that could materially affect an employee, customer, supplier, financial outcome, or regulatory obligation will retain appropriate human review and approval.

## Scope

The initial solution will be available through a secure web interface and, where practical, through the organization’s existing collaboration and productivity platforms. It will use single sign-on, role-based access, and permission-aware retrieval so that responses are generated only from information the requesting employee is authorized to access. Responses will identify their sources wherever possible, allowing users to verify important information.

The first release will connect to priority knowledge repositories such as the intranet, policy library, document management platform, service desk knowledge base, HR guidance, finance procedures, and selected operational wikis. Additional sources will be added only after their ownership, data quality, access controls, retention requirements, and suitability for AI retrieval have been reviewed.

Core capabilities will include enterprise search and question answering, document summarization, drafting and rewriting, meeting and project preparation, policy navigation, and guided completion of selected service requests. The assistant may recommend actions or prepare submissions, but transactions and other consequential actions will require explicit user confirmation and, where appropriate, approval by a designated employee.

The technical design will use an approved model gateway, retrieval and search services, content filtering, prompt and response safeguards, audit logging, monitoring, and data-loss-prevention controls. Organizational data will not be used to train external foundation models unless expressly approved through the organization’s legal, privacy, security, and procurement processes. Sensitive information will be minimized, protected in transit and at rest, and handled according to existing classification and retention standards.

The project includes user research, data-source preparation, solution design, integration, testing, security and privacy assessment, pilot deployment, organization-wide rollout, training, communications, support, and performance measurement. It does not include a broad replacement of existing enterprise applications or the immediate automation of every business process.

## Delivery Approach and Governance

The initiative will be sponsored by the CIO or equivalent executive, with active participation from business leadership, information security, privacy, legal, human resources, records management, and employee representatives where required. An AI steering committee will set priorities, approve high-risk use cases, resolve policy questions, and review performance and incidents.

A dedicated product team will manage the assistant as an ongoing enterprise service rather than a one-time technology implementation. Business data owners will remain accountable for the quality and authorization of the content made available to the assistant. Each connected source will have an identified owner, a documented refresh schedule, and a process for correcting inaccurate or outdated information.

Before each release, the team will conduct functional testing, access-control testing, prompt-injection and data-exfiltration testing, privacy review, usability testing, and evaluation against a representative benchmark of organizational questions. The service will provide a clear mechanism for employees to report incorrect, unsafe, or inappropriate responses. High-severity issues will be subject to defined incident-response procedures, including the ability to suspend a connector or capability quickly.

Change management will be treated as a core workstream. Employees will receive practical guidance on appropriate use, limitations, confidentiality, verification of responses, and escalation procedures. A network of departmental champions will demonstrate relevant use cases, gather feedback, and help teams adopt the assistant responsibly. Training will be supplemented by an internal help channel, user documentation, and regular communications describing new capabilities and known limitations.

## Timeline

The project will be delivered over twelve months in five connected phases.

During the first four weeks, the organization will mobilize the program, appoint the executive sponsor and product owner, confirm governance, identify priority use cases, assess the current data and technology landscape, and establish baseline measures for productivity, service demand, employee experience, and information-search time. This phase will also define the initial risk classification and approve the sources and user groups for the pilot.

From weeks five through twelve, the team will design and build the minimum viable service. This work will include selecting the model and platform approach, configuring identity and access controls, preparing the first knowledge sources, developing the assistant experience, establishing monitoring and analytics, and completing the initial security and privacy reviews. A curated evaluation set will be created to measure answer quality, citation accuracy, access control, and harmful or misleading outputs.

From weeks thirteen through eighteen, the assistant will be piloted with approximately 250 to 400 employees representing corporate functions, operational teams, managers, and a range of technical skill levels. The pilot will focus on low- and medium-risk use cases, such as policy questions, enterprise search, summarization, drafting, and service-desk guidance. Feedback, usage data, and evaluation results will be used to improve retrieval quality, prompts, user guidance, and support processes.

From weeks nineteen through thirty, the service will expand to approximately 2,000 employees in successive waves. Each wave will add validated data sources and business scenarios only after the preceding wave meets agreed quality, security, and adoption thresholds. Targeted training, office hours, and departmental champions will support each expansion.

From weeks thirty-one through fifty-two, the assistant will be made available across the organization, subject to the results of the preceding phases. The final portion of the year will focus on optimization, additional integrations, cost management, workflow enhancements, and the transition from project delivery to steady-state product operations. At the end of the first year, the steering committee will review benefits, risks, adoption, and the roadmap for the following year.

## Resource Requirements

The initiative will require a core team of approximately twelve to fifteen full-time equivalent roles during design, implementation, and rollout. The team should include an executive sponsor, product owner, program manager, enterprise architect, AI or machine-learning engineer, software and integration engineers, data and search specialists, security and privacy representatives, user-experience and research support, change and training leads, and a service-support analyst. Several of these roles may be supplied by existing teams rather than hired specifically for the project.

The core team will be supported by part-time representatives from HR, IT, finance, legal, information governance, communications, procurement, and major business functions. These subject-matter experts will identify high-value use cases, validate content, review responses, define escalation paths, and participate in pilot evaluation. A network of approximately twenty to thirty departmental champions should be established before the broader rollout.

Technology resources will include an approved generative AI model or model portfolio, a secure orchestration layer, enterprise search or vector retrieval capabilities, data connectors, content-filtering and safety services, identity and access-management integration, logging and observability, a testing environment, and support for usage and cost analytics. The organization should maintain the flexibility to change models without redesigning the entire application, reducing dependency on a single provider.

The first-year budget should cover platform and model consumption, integration and development, security testing, data preparation, user research, training, communications, support, and contingency for additional controls or infrastructure. The final funding request should be confirmed during the discovery phase after the organization selects its deployment model and identifies the number and complexity of required integrations.

## Success Criteria

The project will be considered successful when the assistant is available to all employees for approved use cases, operates within documented security and privacy controls, and demonstrates measurable value compared with current ways of working.

By the end of the first year, the target is for at least 65 percent of employees to use the assistant monthly, with at least 75 percent of pilot and early-wave users returning to it regularly after their first interaction. User satisfaction should reach an average of at least 4 out of 5, and a clear majority of users should report that the assistant helps them find information or complete routine work more quickly.

For quality, at least 85 percent of responses in the approved evaluation benchmark should be materially correct, and at least 90 percent of responses requiring organizational knowledge should provide an accurate and relevant source or clearly state that no verified answer was found. The assistant should demonstrate a measurable reduction in the median time employees spend locating internal information, with an initial target of 20 percent in the pilot use cases. Selected service functions should achieve a reduction of at least 15 percent in repetitive, low-complexity requests without reducing employee satisfaction or increasing unresolved escalations.

Security and compliance are non-negotiable measures of success. There should be no critical incidents involving unauthorized disclosure of organizational or personal information. All production data sources must have documented ownership and access controls, all high-risk use cases must have human-approval points, and all material incidents must be logged, investigated, and resolved under an approved response process. Service reliability should meet an agreed enterprise standard, with a target of at least 99.5 percent availability during normal operating hours and acceptable response times for routine queries.

Finally, the organization should be able to demonstrate that the service is financially and operationally sustainable. Usage and model costs must be visible, the cost per active user must remain within the approved business case, support volumes must be manageable, and the product team must have a prioritized roadmap for continued improvement.

## Conclusion

Deploying an internal AI assistant across a 5,000-employee organization is both a technology initiative and an operating-model change. A phased, governed approach will allow the organization to capture immediate productivity benefits while protecting confidential information, preserving human accountability, and building employee trust. Approval is requested to begin the four-week mobilization and discovery phase, establish the governance structure, confirm the initial use cases and data sources, and return with a detailed implementation plan and final budget for the pilot.

An internal AI assistant could support employees without replacing professional judgment or existing systems of record. It would serve as a governed access layer across approved organizational knowledge, providing answers with links to source material and helping employees draft, summarize, analyze, and prepare work products.

This proposal recommends a phased, 12-month deployment of an internal AI assistant for the organization’s 5,000 employees. The initiative will prioritize security, privacy, accuracy, accessibility, transparency, and measurable business value. The assistant will be introduced through controlled pilots, expanded based on evidence, and supported by clear governance and employee training.

## Objectives

The primary objective is to improve employee productivity and access to organizational knowledge while maintaining the organization’s standards for information security, privacy, compliance, and responsible technology use.

The assistant will provide a single, intuitive interface through which employees can ask questions about approved internal content, locate policies and procedures, summarize documents, draft routine communications, generate meeting preparation materials, and receive guidance on internal processes. Where appropriate, it will connect employees to existing systems such as the intranet, document repositories, collaboration platforms, service-management tools, and approved business applications.

The initiative will also establish a repeatable enterprise capability for adopting AI responsibly. This will include data and access controls, model and vendor oversight, usage policies, auditability, human review requirements, content ownership, and a process for evaluating new use cases. The assistant will be designed to augment employees rather than make unsupervised decisions about people, finances, legal matters, safety, employment, or other high-impact activities.

The program will seek to reduce time spent searching for information and completing repetitive knowledge work, improve consistency in the use of internal policies and processes, increase employee access to expertise, and create a foundation for future AI-enabled capabilities.

## Scope

The initial solution will be an enterprise web and mobile-accessible assistant integrated with the organization’s identity and access-management platform. Employees will sign in using existing corporate credentials, and the assistant will enforce the same role-based permissions that govern access to source systems. It will not expose documents or information to an employee merely because the assistant can retrieve them; access will remain subject to the employee’s existing authorization.

The assistant’s first release will support secure question answering over approved internal content, document and meeting summarization, drafting and rewriting, information comparison, policy and process guidance, and assistance with common IT, HR, finance, procurement, and operational questions. Responses will identify their supporting sources whenever feasible, clearly distinguish retrieved organizational information from generated content, and advise employees when human review is required.

The deployment will include integrations with the organization’s primary knowledge repositories and collaboration tools, such as the intranet, document-management platform, approved shared drives, knowledge bases, and service-management systems. Content owners will be responsible for identifying authoritative sources, resolving duplicate or outdated material, defining retention requirements, and approving content for use by the assistant.

The program will establish an enterprise AI governance framework covering privacy, cybersecurity, records management, accessibility, procurement, legal review, acceptable use, model risk, incident response, and vendor management. Usage and performance data will be collected in accordance with applicable policies and laws, with appropriate controls for sensitive information.

The initial scope will not include fully autonomous actions in business systems, unsupervised decisions affecting employees or customers, generation of binding legal or financial advice, or the use of unapproved external tools with confidential organizational data. Any future expansion into transactional or high-impact use cases will require separate risk assessment, business approval, testing, and governance review.

## Implementation Approach and Timeline

The initiative will be delivered over approximately 12 months in five stages, followed by continuous improvement.

During Months 1 and 2, the organization will establish the program foundation. This stage will confirm the executive sponsor, appoint the product owner, define governance and decision rights, assess current information architecture, identify priority use cases, and establish baseline measures for productivity, employee experience, service volumes, and information-retrieval time. The organization will also evaluate available platform and model options, complete an initial privacy and security assessment, define technical and procurement requirements, and select the first internal content sources.

During Months 3 and 4, the delivery team will build the minimum viable platform. This work will include identity integration, permission enforcement, logging, content ingestion, retrieval and citation capabilities, model configuration, user-interface development, monitoring, and administrative controls. Security testing, privacy review, accessibility testing, and responsible-use guidance will be completed before any employee pilot. Training materials and communications will be prepared in parallel.

During Months 5 and 6, the assistant will be piloted with approximately 300 to 500 employees representing different functions, levels, locations, and technology needs. The pilot will focus on high-value, relatively low-risk use cases such as internal search, policy questions, drafting, summarization, and meeting preparation. Pilot participants will receive training and clear instructions on appropriate use. Their feedback, task-completion data, answer-quality ratings, support requests, and security findings will be used to refine the solution.

During Months 7 through 9, the assistant will be expanded to approximately 1,500 employees across priority business units. Additional content sources and integrations will be introduced only after validation. The organization will refine prompts, retrieval methods, source-content governance, user guidance, and support processes. A formal readiness review will determine whether the solution meets the security, reliability, usability, and value thresholds required for enterprise deployment.

During Months 10 through 12, the assistant will be rolled out to the remaining employees in waves. Communications will emphasize the assistant’s capabilities, limitations, data-handling rules, and requirement for human judgment. Managers and subject-matter experts will receive additional guidance so they can support adoption and identify opportunities for improvement. At the end of the first year, the program will conduct a benefits review and publish a roadmap for the next phase, which may include additional integrations, workflow support, or carefully governed transactional capabilities.

## Resource Requirements

The program will require an executive sponsor with authority across business, technology, risk, and corporate functions. A dedicated product owner and program manager will coordinate priorities, delivery, communications, and benefits realization. The core implementation team should include an enterprise architect, AI or machine-learning engineers, application and integration engineers, data and content specialists, information-security personnel, privacy and legal representatives, user-experience and accessibility specialists, change-management and training leads, and service-desk support.

A core team of approximately 12 to 18 full-time-equivalent personnel is expected during implementation, supplemented by part-time representatives from HR, legal, compliance, records management, finance, IT, information security, communications, and major business units. Each participating business function should designate content owners and subject-matter experts who can validate source material, identify priority use cases, and review high-risk responses.

The technology environment will require an enterprise-grade foundation model or approved model service, secure hosting, identity and access management, document and content connectors, retrieval and indexing capabilities, monitoring, audit logging, data-loss-prevention controls, and service-management integration. The selected vendor or platform must provide contractual protections for organizational data, including clear limitations on model training, defined data retention, regional hosting options where required, incident-notification obligations, and appropriate service-level commitments.

The organization should also fund employee education, communications, pilot incentives, accessibility support, content remediation, and ongoing model and security testing. The implementation budget will depend on the selected model, hosting approach, usage volume, integration complexity, and degree of content remediation. A detailed cost estimate will be prepared during the foundation stage, with separate estimates for implementation, licensing, infrastructure, training, and ongoing operations.

## Governance and Operating Model

The assistant will operate under a cross-functional governance board responsible for policy, risk acceptance, use-case prioritization, vendor oversight, and expansion decisions. The board will establish an approved-use policy explaining what employees may enter into the assistant, how generated content must be reviewed, when human expertise is mandatory, and how suspected errors or harmful outputs should be reported.

The operating model will assign clear ownership for the assistant platform, each connected content source, response quality, security monitoring, privacy compliance, and employee support. Automated testing and regular evaluations will measure factual accuracy, citation quality, bias, inappropriate disclosure, prompt-injection resistance, and performance across representative employee tasks. The organization will maintain an incident process for inaccurate answers, unauthorized disclosure, harmful recommendations, or service failures.

The assistant will be positioned as a support tool, not an authoritative decision-maker. Employees will remain accountable for verifying important information and following existing approval, legal, financial, employment, safety, and records-management requirements.

## Success Criteria

The initiative will be considered successful if, within six months of the organization-wide rollout, at least 70 percent of employees have activated the assistant and at least 50 percent of employees in the target user population use it monthly. Adoption will be evaluated alongside quality and business outcomes rather than treated as the sole measure of success.

The solution should achieve an average employee usefulness rating of at least 80 percent for supported use cases, provide source citations for at least 90 percent of answers based on internal content, and maintain service availability of at least 99.5 percent during business hours. Median response time for standard requests should remain within an acceptable enterprise service target, with performance monitored by use case and peak demand.

The program should demonstrate a measurable reduction in time spent locating information, preparing routine drafts, summarizing materials, and answering recurring internal questions. The initial target is a 20 percent reduction in time for selected pilot workflows, validated through baseline and post-deployment studies. Participating service teams should also report a reduction in repetitive information requests and an increase in the proportion of requests resolved through self-service.

No critical security or privacy incident attributable to the assistant will be accepted. All production use will be covered by access controls, audit logging, approved data-handling rules, and documented incident-response procedures. The organization should achieve completion of required responsible-use training for at least 90 percent of active users within the first six months of broad deployment.

At the end of the first year, the executive sponsor and governance board will review adoption, employee experience, productivity gains, operational cost, risk events, content quality, and support demand. Continued investment and expansion will be based on demonstrated value, sustained employee trust, and evidence that the assistant is operating securely and responsibly at enterprise scale.

# Project Proposal: Enterprise Internal AI Assistant

## Background and Rationale

The organization’s 5,000 employees rely on a growing collection of intranet pages, policy documents, knowledge bases, collaboration spaces, service-desk records, and business applications. Although this information is valuable, it is often difficult to locate, interpret, and apply. Employees spend significant time searching across systems, repeating questions, drafting routine communications, summarizing information, and navigating standard HR and IT processes. This creates avoidable operating costs and inconsistent employee experiences.

At the same time, employees are increasingly using publicly available generative AI tools to complete these tasks. Unmanaged use introduces risks related to confidential information, privacy, intellectual property, inaccurate advice, and regulatory compliance. The organization therefore has an opportunity to provide a secure, governed alternative that improves productivity while protecting company and employee data.

This proposal recommends the phased deployment of an internal AI assistant that gives employees conversational access to approved organizational knowledge, supports common drafting and summarization tasks, and enables selected low-risk business workflows. The assistant will be designed as a productivity and knowledge-access tool, not as a replacement for expert judgment, established approval processes, or accountable business owners.

## Objectives

The primary objective is to provide every employee with secure, reliable, and easy-to-use access to an AI assistant that can help them find information, understand policies, create first drafts, summarize content, and complete routine tasks more efficiently.

Second, it will improve the consistency and accessibility of internal guidance by presenting answers grounded in approved company sources and linking users back to the relevant documents. Third, it will reduce avoidable demand on HR, IT, service-desk, and other support teams by handling appropriate frequently asked questions and standard requests. Fourth, it will establish the governance, technical foundation, and operating model required for responsible use of artificial intelligence across the organization.

Initial performance targets will include a 15 percent reduction in time spent locating information and a 20 percent reduction in time spent on selected drafting and summarization tasks among pilot users. For connected HR and IT use cases, the organization will target a 20 to 30 percent reduction in repetitive tier-one inquiries, subject to baseline measurements and service-quality safeguards.

## Scope

The project will deliver an enterprise AI assistant accessible through a web application and, where appropriate, the organization’s primary collaboration platform, such as Microsoft Teams or Slack. Employees will authenticate through the existing identity and access-management environment. The assistant will enforce source-system permissions so that users can retrieve and receive only information they are authorized to access.

An executive steering committee will set priorities and resolve cross-functional issues, while an operational AI governance group will oversee risk assessments, use-case approvals, data access, model evaluation, incident response, and policy updates. A dedicated product team will manage the roadmap, service performance, user experience, and value realization.

The assistant will communicate its limitations and direct users to authoritative sources or human experts when confidence is low, source information conflicts, or a request falls into a restricted category. High-impact use cases will require documented human accountability and additional review. All material incidents, including inaccurate answers with business impact, inappropriate access, privacy concerns, or unsafe automated actions, will be logged, investigated, and used to improve the service.

## Success Criteria

The project will be considered successful when the assistant is available to all 5,000 employees, operates within approved security and privacy controls, and demonstrates measurable business value. Within six months of full deployment, the target is for at least 60 percent of employees to use the assistant monthly, with sustained weekly use among a substantial share of knowledge workers and service-oriented teams.

Quality will be measured through a continuously maintained benchmark of representative employee questions. At least 85 percent of benchmark responses should be accurate, appropriately grounded in approved sources, and accompanied by usable citations, with zero unresolved critical data-access failures. For high-impact or restricted requests, the system must consistently refuse, escalate, or require human review as designed. Production availability should reach at least 99.5 percent, and standard responses should normally be delivered within an acceptable employee-facing response time.

Business impact will be assessed against the baselines established before the pilot. The organization will seek at least a 15 percent reduction in information-search time, a 20 percent improvement in efficiency for selected drafting and summarization tasks, and a 20 to 30 percent reduction in repetitive HR and IT inquiries where the assistant is connected to those services. Employee satisfaction with the experience should reach at least 80 percent among active users, while support teams should report no material decline in service quality or employee trust.

Finally, the organization must demonstrate responsible operation. This means complete authentication and authorization coverage, auditable use of connected data, documented ownership for all production knowledge sources, effective incident response, completion of required employee training, and no critical privacy or security breach attributable to the assistant. A positive return on investment should be validated within 12 to 18 months of full deployment through measured productivity gains, reduced support demand, improved knowledge reuse, and avoidance of unmanaged AI-tool costs and risks.

Deploying the internal AI assistant through this phased, governed approach will allow the organization to capture immediate productivity benefits while building the capabilities needed for broader and more sophisticated uses of artificial intelligence over time.
